skill against repo standards and validators;\\n- compare two skill variants;\\n- package a validated skill for reuse;\\n- improve skill-graph contracts tied to recursive workflow operations.\\n\\nDo not use this skill for unrelated application features, generic debugging, or ordinary documentation tasks that do not create or improve a skill.\\n\\n## LearningPosture compatibility\\n\\nThis skill must preserve existing `delegation.mode` semantics while supporting posture-aware guidance via `learning_posture` metadata.\\n\\n- Supported posture modes:\\n  - `learn`: explain alternatives, assumptions, and risks first before proposing edits.\\n  - `guided`: propose concrete improvements, keep the user in the loop, and require explicit progression checkpoints.\\n  - `execute`: apply agreed changes only after scope, inputs, and safety gates are present.\\n- Default posture for this skill is `guided`.\\n- Explicit `learn` posture requests should delay output-only behavior and increase explanation depth.\\n- For execution requests, the skill should still preserve the advisory safety bar and never remove existing human checkpoint gates from the spec.\\n\\n## Modes\\nChoose the smallest mode that fits:\\n- **create**: scaffold and author a new skill;\\n- **improve**: tighten routing, workflow, safety, or portability;\\n- **eval**: run validators and summarize upstream-grade and gold-grade status.\\n- Emit one decision per skill: `pass`, `warn`, or `fail`, with a short reason and next fix.\\n\\n## Needed inputs\\n- skill goal;\\n- 3-10 example prompts:\\n Covers `harness init`, harness-managed CI migration, governance checks, and Codex environment action-sync guidance. Do not use for unrelated coding, general deployment, or broad cloud work.\\nmetadata:\\n  skill-type: team_automation\\n---\\n\\n# Coding Harness\\nOperate `@brainwav/coding-harness` with command-accurate setup flows, conservative mutation rules, and explicit governance boundaries.\\n\\n## Table of Contents\\n- [When to use](#when-to-use)\\n- [Required inputs](#required-inputs)\\n- [Deliverables](#deliverables)\\n- [Philosophy](#philosophy)\\n- [Workflow](#workflow)\\n- [Validation](#validation)\\n- [References](#references)\\n- [Constraints and safety](#constraints-and-safety)\\n- [Anti-patterns](#anti-patterns)\\n- [Failure mode](#failure-mode)\\n- [Gotchas](#gotchas)\\n- [Examples](#examples)\\n- [See Also](#see-also)\\n\\n## When to use\\nUse this skill when the request is to:\\n- install `@brainwav/coding-harness` in a repository and verify the scaffold safely;\\n- bootstrap or repair `harness init`, including preview, update, migrate, and rollback paths;\\n- explain what coding-harness can and cannot do, including required tokens, remote-check boundaries, and environment setup;\\n- audit whether `.codex/environments/environment.toml` action blocks are aligned with current project scripts;\\n- guide or execute GitHub Actions to CircleCI cutover using `harness ci-migrate` instead of manual workflow deletion.\\n\\nDo not use this skill for:\\n- unrelated application feature work;\\n- generic cloud deployment work that is not about harness governance;\\n- broad security reviews that are not tied to coding-harness install, policy, or verification surfaces.\\n- ordinary questions or creative tasks that do not involve coding-harness. In those cases, answer normally or route to a more relevant skill.\\n\\n## Required inputs\\n- target repository path and package-manager context;\\n- current harness state: `not installed`, `installed`, `needs update`, or `broken`;\\n- execution posture: `no-execution` guidance or command-running execution mode;\\n- auth posture for remote checks, such as PAT or GitHub App JWT, when `verify-greptile` or similar remote checks are requested;\\n- desired verification depth: lightweight setup confirmation or deep runtime/artifact validation.\\n\\nIf details are missing, make the safest reasonable assumption:\\n- default to no-execution mode for explanation-only asks;\\n- default to preview-first commands before mutative operations;\\n- default to skipping remote checks until the user provides auth material.\\n\\n## Deliverables\\nProduce only what the request needs, usually:\\n- a setup or remediation summary with exact commands run;\\n- a file-level change summary when harness scaffolds or updates repository files;\\n- a validation ladder summary that distinguishes baseline gates, deep gates, and conditional harness-specific checks;\\n- a capability boundary summary covering `can do`, `cannot do`, and `requires user-provided auth`;\\n- explicit pass/fail evidence plus the next safe action when anything remains unresolved;\\n- machine-readable reports that preserve `schema_version` whenever the output is schema-bound.\\n\\n## Philosophy\\n- Prefer deterministic, evidence-backed setup over assumptions.\\n- Keep installation and update guidance reversible, preview-first, and command-accurate.\\n- Treat capability boundaries as part of the contract, especially around auth, destructive changes, and enforced scaffold files.\\n- Separate `skill bundle is accurate` from `target repo is fully green` because those are different claims.\\n- When refusing unsafe or unsupported requests, say `cannot` plainly and explain the missing evidence or prerequisite.\\n\\n## Workflow\\n1. Confirm execution mode.\\n- Do stay in no-execution mode when the user wants explanation or planning because that keeps guidance reversible.\\n- Do switch to execution mode only when command evidence is required because completion claims must be grounded in the live repo state.\\n\\n2. Preflight the repository.\\n- Do confirm repo root, toolchain availability, and current harness state because path-sensitive or multi-step work is fragile without preflight.\\n- Do run `source scripts/codex-preflight.sh && preflight_repo` when available because harness-enabled repos often encode extra local policy there.\\n\\n3. Install or upgrade harness conservatively.\\n- Do prefer `mise install -g npm:@brainwav/coding-harness` for consumer repos because it matches the current recommended global install posture.\\n- Do bootstrap with `harness init --dry-run` followed by `harness init` because the current CLI-safe path is preview-first.\\n- Do not pass `--ci circleci` to `harness init` because the current CLI treats the extra positional token as a target directory in this flow.\\n- Do use `harness ci-migrate prepare --provider circleci --dry-run`, then `--apply`, `verify --snapshot <snapshot-id>`, `commit --snapshot <snapshot-id>`, and `abort --snapshot <snapshot-id>` because cutover must stay reversible and snapshot-bound.\\n- Do use project-local source execution only when you are actively developing the coding-harness repository because consumer repos should follow the packaged CLI contract.\\n\\n4. Validate setup and policy state.\\n- Do run the baseline repository gate first because `pnpm check` catches the broad integration surface expected by the tool.\\n- Do escalate to `pnpm test:deep` when runtime behavior or artifact formats changed because baseline checks are not enough for behavior-affecting work.\\n- Do use targeted harness checks such as `harness check-environment`, `verify-greptile`, `check-authz`, `docs-gate`, and `tooling-audit` when the user asks for specific governance evidence.\\n- Do rely on structured `--json` output for gates and `health --auto-fix --dry-run` because machine-readable findings are safer to automate than table scraping.\\n- Do answer directly that a repo is not verified yet when checks were skipped because unsupported certainty is worse than an incomplete status.\\n\\n5. Report capability boundaries explicitly.\\n- Do say which checks were actually run because remote verification and auth-dependent gates are optional until credentials exist.\\n- Do call out user-managed surfaces such as secrets, tokens, branch protection ownership, and non-autogenerated environment files because harness does not replace human authority there.\\n\\n6. Record repo-specific learnings when applicable.\\n- Do read `~/.codex/instructions/Learnings.md` first and `.harness/memory/LEARNINGS.md` second because the skill uses both global and repo-scoped memory.\\n- Do append only repo-specific lessons to `.harness/memory/LEARNINGS.md` when `.harness/` exists because harness repos treat that file as an append-only local knowledge base.\\n\\n## Validation\\nRun the smallest relevant checks first, then broaden before claiming completion:\\n\\n```bash\\nharness --help\\nharness init --dry-run\\npnpm check\\npnpm test:deep\\n```\\n\\nUse targeted governance or lifecycle commands as needed:\\n\\n```bash\\nharness init --check-updates\\nharness init --update\\nharness init --migrate\\nharness init --rollback\\nharness ci-migrate prepare --provider circleci --dry-run\\nharness ci-migrate prepare --provider circleci --apply\\nharness ci-migrate verify --snapshot <snapshot-id>\\nharness ci-migrate commit --snapshot <snapshot-id>\\nharness ci-migrate abort --snapshot <snapshot-id>\\nharness verify-greptile\\nharness verify-greptile --token <token-or-jwt> --owner <owner> --repo <repo>\\nharness check-authz --contract <path> --repo <owner/repo> --branch <branch>\\nharness check-environment --contract <path> --attestation <path>\\nharness docs-gate --mode advisory --json\\nharness tooling-audit --path <dir> --format table\\nharness evidence-verify --files <paths>\\nharness health --auto-fix --dry-run --json\\n```\\n\\nCanonical skill maintenance gates after edits:\\n\\n```bash\\nbash scripts/lint_openai_skill_format.sh --mode strict\\nbash scripts/lint_progressive_disclosure.sh --mode warn\\npython3 scripts/gotcha_pipeline.py validate\\npython3 scripts/check-see-also.py . --changed-files utilities/coding-harness/SKILL.md\\npython3 utilities/skill-builder/scripts/validate_skill_graph_profiles.py --repo-root . --expected-count 0\\nbash scripts/sync_skills_sandbox_safe.sh\\nbash scripts/lint_skill_types.sh\\npython3 utilities/skill-builder/scripts/skill_gate.py utilities/coding-harness --require-fail-fast --require-security-evals\\npython3 utilities/skill-builder/scripts/run_skill_evals.py utilities/coding-harness --eval-mode release --runner codex --capture-jsonl --timeout-profile codex-heavy\\n```\\n\\nFail fast on the first blocking gate, fix the specific issue, rerun that gate, and only then continue to broader validation.\\n\\n## References\\n- `references/agent-install-guide.md`\\n  Read when: you need the human-readable install, update, and CI migration sequence with rollback.\\n- `references/agent-install.json`\\n  Read when: you need machine-readable phases, commands, or scaffolded file lists.\\n- `references/setup-and-commands.md`\\n  Read when: you need the wider command map, lifecycle commands, or CI secret wiring details.\\n- `references/structured-json-output.md`\\n  Read when: you need the `GateResult` schema, `jq` extraction patterns, or `health --auto-fix` usage.\\n- `references/contract.yaml`\\n  Read when: you need the machine-checkable input/output contract for this skill.\\n- `references/evals.yaml`\\n  Read when: you need trigger coverage, adversarial cases, or release-eval inputs.\\n- `references/plan.md`\\n  Read when: you need preserved implementation context from the packaged-skill work rather than the operator-facing wrapper alone.\\n- `agents/openai.yaml`\\n  Read when: you need the display metadata used by external skill packaging surfaces.\\n\\n## Constraints and safety\\n- Redact secrets, tokens, and sensitive repository data in logs, artifacts, and summaries.\\n- Require explicit user confirmation before destructive or high-impact mutations.\\n- Treat `harness --help` as command truth when older docs disagree.\\n- Do not claim full setup success without command evidence from the current repository state.\\n- Treat remote checks as optional until the user provides the required auth material.\\n- Do not hand-edit enforced harness outputs such as `harness.contract.json`, `.circleci/config.yml`, or `scripts/check-environment.sh` because `harness init --update` will overwrite them.\\n- Only auto-update `.codex/environments/environment.toml` when the file is harness-generated because user-owned environment config needs an approval checkpoint.\\n\\n## Anti-patterns\\n- claiming harness is configured without running verification commands;\\n- deleting `.github/workflows/` files manually instead of using `harness ci-migrate`;\\n- treating `pnpm check` and `pnpm test:deep` as interchangeable when runtime behavior changed;\\n- reporting remote verification as passed when auth was never supplied;\\n- applying `harness init --update` without previewing first when repo state is unclear;\\n- editing enforced scaffold files by hand and assuming the changes will persist.\\n\\n## Failure mode\\n- If the target repo path cannot be verified, stop before mutating anything and ask for the exact root.\\n- If auth-dependent checks are requested without credentials, explain the missing prerequisite and continue only with local/non-remote validation.\\n- If command help output conflicts with packaged docs, follow the command output, call out the drift, and repair the canonical copy before claiming completion.\\n- If the repo is already red on unrelated gates, separate `skill bundle is correct` from `repo aggregate is green` instead of overstating success.\\n- If the request is unrelated to coding-harness, do not force this workflow onto it; either answer normally or route to the correct skill.\\n\\n## Gotchas\\n- Symptom: `harness init --ci circleci` fails with a path-resolution error. Cause: the current CLI interprets `circleci` like a target directory in that flow. Do instead: run `harness init --dry-run` and then `harness init`. Check: rerun `harness init --dry-run` and confirm the scaffold plan renders normally.\\n- Symptom: CI migration guidance looks right but rollback is missing. Cause: older summaries often stop after `commit`. Do instead: preserve the full snapshot-based sequence including `abort --snapshot <snapshot-id>`. Check: confirm preview, apply, verify, commit, and abort all appear in both `SKILL.md` and `references/agent-install-guide.md`.\\n- Symptom: an agent claims repo setup is complete after only local checks. Cause: remote gates such as Greptile verification were skipped because auth was missing. Do instead: report the local pass separately from auth-blocked remote checks. verification as passed when auth was never supplied;\\n- applying `harness init --update` without previewing first when repo state is unclear;\\n- editing enforced scaffold files by hand and assuming the changes will persist.\\n\\n## Failure mode\\n- If the target repo path cannot be verified, stop before mutating anything and ask for the exact root.\\n- If auth-dependent checks are requested without credentials, explain the missing prerequisite and continue only with local/non-remote validation.\\n- If command help output conflicts with packaged docs, follow the command output, call out the drift, and repair the canonical copy before claiming completion.\\n- If the repo is already red on unrelated gates, separate `skill bundle is correct` from `repo aggregate is green` instead of overstating success.\\n- If the request is unrelated to coding-harness, do not force this workflow onto it; either answer normally or route to the correct skill.\\n\\n## Gotchas\\n- Symptom: `harness init --ci circleci` fails with a path-resolution error. Cause: the current CLI interprets `circleci` like a target directory in that flow. Do instead: run `harness init --dry-run` and then `harness init`. Check: rerun `harness init --dry-run` and confirm the scaffold plan renders normally.\\n- Symptom: CI migration guidance looks right but rollback is missing. Cause: older summaries often stop after `commit`. Do instead: preserve the full snapshot-based sequence including `abort --snapshot <snapshot-id>`. Check: confirm preview, apply, verify, commit, and abort all appear in both `SKILL.md` and `references/agent-install-guide.md`.\\n- Symptom: an agent claims repo setup is complete after only local checks. Cause: remote gates such as Greptile verification were skipped because auth was missing. Do instead: report the local pass separately from auth-blocked remote checks. Check: the final summary should say exactly which checks were skipped and why.\\n- Symptom: `.harness/memory/LEARNINGS.md` guidance is applied to a repo without `.harness/`. Cause: the memory layer is repo-specific, not universal. Do instead: skip creation when `.harness/` is absent. Check: only read or append the repo memory file when the harness directory exists.\\n\\n## Examples\\n- Triggering prompt: \\\"Set up the Brainwav harness in this repo and tell me what still needs my credentials.\\\"\\n- Triggering prompt: \\\"Show me the safe repo-governance bootstrap flow, including preview, validation, and rollback.\\\"\\n- Triggering prompt: \\\"Audit whether our Codex environment actions are still aligned with the current scripts.\\\"\\n- Non-triggering prompt: \\\"Build a new dashboard for our admin panel.\\\"\\n\\n## See Also\\n| Skill | When to use |\\n|---|---|\\n| [[bootstrap]] | Clone and bootstrap a repository before coding-harness setup begins |\\n| [[circleci]] | Work on CircleCI-specific pipeline design or migration details beyond the harness wrapper |\\n| [[verification-before-completion]] | Add a stronger final verification pass before claiming a repo change is complete |\\n| [[systematic-debugging]] | Root-cause failing harness commands or broken repo state before applying fixes |\\n\\n**Topic map:** [[agent-ops]]\\n\\n\\n---\\n/Users/jamiecraik/dev/Agent-Skills/utilities/circleci/SKILL.md:\\n---\\nname: circleci\\ndescription: Plan, migrate, debug, or harden CircleCI pipelines and related delivery workflows. \\\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/main/references/orchestration-patterns.md\\\",\\n  \\\"type\\\": \\\"file\\\",\\n  \\\"content\\\": \\\"# Orchestration Patterns\\\\n\\\\nReference catalog of agent orchestration patterns this repo endorses, plus anti-patterns to avoid. Read this before adding a new slash command that coordinates multiple personas, or before introducing a new persona that \\\\\\\"wraps\\\\\\\" existing ones.\\\\n\\\\nThe governing rule: **the user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. Personas do not invoke other personas.** Skills are mandatory hops inside a persona's workflow.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Endorsed patterns\\\\n\\\\n### 1. Direct invocation (no orchestration)\\\\n\\\\nSingle persona, single perspective, single artifact. The default and the cheapest option.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nuser → code-reviewer → report → user\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the work is one perspective on one artifact and you can describe it in one sentence.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples:**\\\\n- \\\\\\\"Review this PR\\\\\\\" → `code-reviewer`\\\\n- \\\\\\\"Find security issues in `auth.ts`\\\\\\\" → `security-auditor`\\\\n- \\\\\\\"What tests are missing for the checkout flow?\\\\\\\" → `test-engineer`\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one round trip. The baseline you should always compare orchestrated patterns against.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 2. Single-persona slash command\\\\n\\\\nA slash command that wraps one persona with the project's skills. Saves the user from re-explaining the workflow every time.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n/review → code-reviewer (with code-review-and-quality skill) → report\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the same single-persona invocation happens repeatedly with the same setup.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/review`, `/test`, `/code-simplify`.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** same as direct invocation. The slash command is just a saved prompt.\\\\n\\\\n**Anti-signal:** if the slash command's body is mostly \\\\\\\"decide which persona to call,\\\\\\\" delete it and let the user call the persona directly.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 3. Parallel fan-out with merge\\\\n\\\\nMultiple personas operate on the same input concurrently, each producing an independent report. A merge step (in the main agent's context) synthesizes them into a single decision.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n                    ┌─→ code-reviewer    ─┐\\\\n/ship → fan out  ───┼─→ security-auditor ─┤→ merge → go/no-go + rollback\\\\n                    └─→ test-engineer    ─┘\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\n- The sub-tasks are genuinely independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering dependency)\\\\n- Each sub-agent benefits from its own context window\\\\n- The merge step is small enough to stay in the main context\\\\n- Wall-clock latency matters\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/ship`.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** N parallel sub-agent contexts + one merge turn. Higher than direct invocation, but faster wall-clock and produces better reports because each sub-agent stays focused on its single perspective.\\\\n\\\\n**Validation checklist before adopting this pattern:**\\\\n- [ ] Can I run all sub-agents at the same time without ordering issues?\\\\n- [ ] Does each persona produce a different *kind* of finding, not just the same finding from a different angle?\\\\n- [ ] Will the merge step fit in the main agent's remaining context?\\\\n- [ ] Is the user's wait time long enough that parallelism is actually noticeable?\\\\n\\\\nIf any answer is \\\\\\\"no,\\\\\\\" fall back to direct invocation or a single-persona command.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 4. Sequential pipeline as user-driven slash commands\\\\n\\\\nThe user runs slash commands in a defined order, carrying context (or commit history) between them. There is no orchestrator agent — the user IS the orchestrator.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nuser runs:  /spec  →  /plan  →  /build  →  /test  →  /review  →  /ship\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the workflow has dependencies (each step needs the previous step's output) and human judgment between steps adds value.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** the entire DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP lifecycle.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one sub-agent context per step. Free for the orchestration layer because there is no orchestrator agent.\\\\n\\\\n**Why not automate it:** an LLM \\\\\\\"lifecycle orchestrator\\\\\\\" would (a) lose nuance between steps because it has to summarize for hand-off, (b) skip the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work early, and (c) double the token cost via paraphrasing turns.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 5. Research isolation (context preservation)\\\\n\\\\nWhen a task requires reading large amounts of material that shouldn't pollute the main context, spawn a research sub-agent that returns only a digest.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nmain agent → research sub-agent (reads 50 files) → digest → main agent continues\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\n- The main session needs to stay focused on a downstream task\\\\n- The investigation result is much smaller than the input it consumes\\\\n- The decision quality benefits from the main agent having room to think after\\\\n\\\\n**Examples:** \\\\\\\"Find every call site of this deprecated API across the monorepo,\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\"Summarize what these 30 ADRs say about caching.\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one isolated sub-agent context. Worth it any time the alternative is loading hundreds of files into the main context.\\\\n\\\\n**On Claude Code, use the built-in `Explore` subagent** rather than defining a custom research persona. `Explore` runs on Haiku, is denied write/edit tools, and is purpose-built for this pattern. Define a custom research subagent only when `Explore` doesn't fit (e.g. you need a domain-specific system prompt the model wouldn't infer).\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Claude Code compatibility\\\\n\\\\nThis catalog is harness-agnostic, but most readers will run it on Claude Code. Here's how each pattern maps onto Claude Code's primitives — and where the platform enforces our rules for us.\\\\n\\\\n### Where personas live\\\\n\\\\nPlugin subagents go in `agents/` at the plugin root. This repo is a plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), so `agents/code-reviewer.md`, `agents/security-auditor.md`, and `agents/test-engineer.md` are auto-discovered when the plugin is enabled. No path configuration needed.\\\\n\\\\n### Subagents vs. Agent Teams\\\\n\\\\nClaude Code has two parallelism primitives. Pattern 3 (parallel fan-out with merge) maps to **subagents**. If you need teammates that talk to each other, use **Agent Teams** instead.\\\\n\\\\n| | Subagents | Agent Teams |\\\\n|--|-----------|-------------|\\\\n| Coordination | Main agent fans out, sub-agents only report back | Teammates message each other, share a task list |\\\\n| Context | Own context window per subagent | Own context window per teammate |\\\\n| When to use | Independent tasks producing reports | Collaborative work needing discussion |\\\\n| Status | Stable | Experimental — requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` |\\\\n| Cost | Lower | Higher — each teammate is a separate Claude instance |\\\\n\\\\n**The personas in this repo work in both modes.** When spawned as subagents (e.g. by `/ship`), they report findings to the main session. When spawned as teammates (`Spawn a teammate using the security-auditor agent type…`), they can challenge each other's findings directly. The persona definition is the same; only the spawning context changes.\\\\n\\\\nOne subtlety: the `skills` and `mcpServers` frontmatter fields in a persona are honored when it runs as a subagent but **ignored when it runs as a teammate** — teammates load skills and MCP servers from your project and user settings, the same as a regular session. If a persona depends on a specific skill or MCP server being loaded, configure it at the session level so it's available in both modes.\\\\n\\\\n### Platform-enforced rules\\\\n\\\\nTwo rules in this catalog aren't just convention — Claude Code enforces them:\\\\n\\\\n- **\\\\\\\"Subagents cannot spawn other subagents\\\\\\\"** (verbatim from the docs). Anti-pattern B (persona-calls-persona) and Anti-pattern D (deep persona trees) cannot exist on Claude Code by construction.\\\\n- **\\\\\\\"No nested teams\\\\\\\"** — teammates cannot spawn their own teams. Same anti-patterns blocked at the team level.\\\\n\\\\nThis means you can adopt the patterns in this catalog without worrying about contributors accidentally building the anti-patterns. They'll just fail to load.\\\\n\\\\n### Built-in subagents to know about\\\\n\\\\nBefore defining a custom subagent, check whether one of these covers the role:\\\\n\\\\n| Built-in | Purpose |\\\\n|----------|---------|\\\\n| `Explore` | Read-only codebase search and analysis. Use this for Pattern 5 (research isolation). |\\\\n| `Plan` | Read-only research during plan mode. |\\\\n| `general-purpose` | Multi-step tasks needing both exploration and modification. |\\\\n\\\\nDon't redefine these. Layer your specialist personas (code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-engineer) on top of them.\\\\n\\\\n### Frontmatter restrictions for plugin agents\\\\n\\\\nPlugin subagents do **not** support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields — these are silently ignored. If a future persona needs any of those, the user must copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` instead.\\\\n\\\\nThe fields that DO work in plugin agents are: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation`, `color`, `initialPrompt`. Use `model` per-persona if you want to optimize cost (e.g. Haiku for `test-engineer` coverage scans, Sonnet for `code-reviewer`, Opus for `security-auditor`).\\\\n\\\\n### Spawning multiple subagents in parallel\\\\n\\\\nIn Claude Code, parallel fan-out (Pattern 3) requires issuing **multiple Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn**. Sequential turns serialize execution. `/ship` calls this out explicitly. Any new orchestrator command should do the same.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Worked example: Agent Teams for competing-hypothesis debugging\\\\n\\\\nThis example shows when to reach for **Agent Teams** instead of `/ship`'s subagent fan-out. The two patterns look similar from a distance — both spawn the same three personas — but the value comes from a different place.\\\\n\\\\n### The scenario\\\\n\\\\n> *Checkout occasionally hangs for ~30 seconds before completing. It happens roughly once every 50 sessions. No errors in logs. Started after last week's release.*\\\\n\\\\nPlausible root causes (mutually exclusive, all fit the symptoms):\\\\n\\\\n1. A race condition in the new payment-confirmation flow\\\\n2. An auth check that occasionally falls through to a slow synchronous network call\\\\n3. A missing index on a query that scales with cart size\\\\n4. A flaky third-party API where the SDK retries silently before timing out\\\\n\\\\nA single agent will pick the first plausible theory and stop investigating. A `/ship`-style subagent fan-out would have each persona report independently — but their reports never meet, so nothing rules out the wrong theories.\\\\n\\\\nThis is exactly the case the Agent Teams docs describe: *\\\\\\\"With multiple independent investigators actively trying to disprove each other, the theory that survives is much more likely to be the actual root cause.\\\\\\\"*\\\\n\\\\n### Why this is *not* a `/ship` job\\\\n\\\\n| | `/ship` (subagents) | Agent Teams |\\\\n|--|--------------------|-------------|\\\\n| Sub-agents see | The same diff, different lenses | A shared task list, each other's messages |\\\\n| Output | Three independent reports → one merge | Adversarial debate → consensus root cause |\\\\n| Right when | You want a verdict on a known artifact | You want to *find* the artifact among hypotheses |\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` is a verdict; Agent Teams is an investigation.\\\\n\\\\n### Setup (one-time, per-environment)\\\\n\\\\nAgent Teams is experimental. In `~/.claude/settings.json`:\\\\n\\\\n```json\\\\n{\\\\n  \\\\\\\"env\\\\\\\": {\\\\n    \\\\\\\"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"1\\\\\\\"\\\\n  }\\\\n}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nRequires Claude Code v2.1.32 or later. The personas in this repo are picked up automatically — no team-config files to author by hand.\\\\n\\\\n### The trigger prompt\\\\n\\\\nType into the lead session, in natural language:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nUsers report checkout hangs for ~30 seconds intermittently after last\\\\nweek's release. No errors in logs.\\\\n\\\\nCreate an agent team to debug this with competing hypotheses. Spawn\\\\nthree teammates using the existing agent types:\\\\n\\\\n  - code-reviewer  — investigate race conditions and blocking calls\\\\n                     in the checkout code path\\\\n  - security-auditor — investigate auth checks, session handling,\\\\n                       and any synchronous network calls added recently\\\\n  - test-engineer  — propose tests that would distinguish between the\\\\n                     hypotheses and check coverage gaps in checkout\\\\n\\\\nHave them message each other directly to challenge each other's\\\\ntheories. Update findings as consensus emerges. Only converge when\\\\ntwo teammates agree they can disprove the others'.\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe lead spawns three teammates referencing the existing persona names. The persona body is **appended** to each teammate's system prompt as additional instructions (on top of the team-coordination instructions the lead installs); the trigger prompt above becomes their task.\\\\n\\\\n### What happens\\\\n\\\\n1. Each teammate runs in its own context window, exploring the codebase from its own lens.\\\\n2. Teammates use `message` to send findings to each other directly. The lead doesn't have to relay.\\\\n3. The shared task list shows who's investigating what — visible at any time with `Ctrl+T` (in-process mode) or in a tmux pane (split mode).\\\\n4. When `code-reviewer` finds a `Promise.all` that should be sequential, it messages `security-auditor` to confirm the auth call isn't part of the race. `security-auditor` checks and replies — either confirming the race is the real issue or producing counter-evidence.\\\\n5. `test-engineer` proposes a focused integration test for whichever theory is winning, which the team uses to verify before declaring consensus.\\\\n6. The lead synthesizes the converged finding and presents it to you.\\\\n\\\\nYou can interrupt at any teammate by cycling with `Shift+Down` and typing — useful for redirecting an investigator who's gone down a wrong path.\\\\n\\\\n### When to clean up\\\\n\\\\nWhen the investigation lands on a root cause, tell the lead:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nClean up the team\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAlways cleanup through the lead, not a teammate (per the docs: teammates lack full team context for cleanup).\\\\n\\\\n### Cost expectation\\\\n\\\\nThree Sonnet teammates running for ~10–15 minutes of investigation costs noticeably more than the same three personas spawned as subagents by `/ship`. The justification is *quality of conclusion* — for production debugging where the wrong fix is expensive, the extra tokens are a bargain. For a routine PR review, stick with `/ship`.\\\\n\\\\n### Anti-pattern in this scenario\\\\n\\\\nDo **not** rebuild this as a `/debug` slash command that fans out subagents. Subagents can't message each other — you'd lose the adversarial debate that makes the pattern work. If a workflow keeps coming up, document the trigger prompt above as a snippet rather than wrapping it in a slash command that misuses subagents.\\\\n\\\\n### When *not* to use Agent Teams\\\\n\\\\n- Production-bound verdict on a known diff → use `/ship` (subagents).\\\\n- One specialist perspective on one artifact → direct persona invocation.\\\\n- Sequential lifecycle (spec → plan → build) → user-driven slash commands (Pattern 4).\\\\n- Read-heavy research with a small digest → built-in `Explore` subagent.\\\\n\\\\nReach for Agent Teams only when teammates **need** to challenge each other to produce the right answer.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Anti-patterns\\\\n\\\\n### A. Router persona (\\\\\\\"meta-orchestrator\\\\\\\")\\\\n\\\\nA persona whose job is to decide which other persona to call.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n/work → router-persona → \\\\\\\"this needs a review\\\\\\\" → code-reviewer → router (paraphrases) → user\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\\\\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + roughly 2× token cost\\\\n- The user already knew they wanted a review; they could have called `/review` directly\\\\n- Replicates the work that slash commands and intent mapping in `AGENTS.md` already do\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** add or refine slash commands. Document intent → command mapping in `AGENTS.md`.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### B. Persona that calls another persona\\\\n\\\\nA `code-reviewer` that internally invokes `security-auditor` when it sees auth code.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Personas were designed to produce a single perspective; chaining them defeats that\\\\n- The summary the calling persona passes loses context the called persona needs\\\\n- Failure modes multiply (which persona's output format wins? whose rules apply?)\\\\n- Hides cost from the user\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** have the calling persona *recommend* a follow-up audit in its report. The user or a slash command runs the second pass.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### C. Sequential orchestrator that paraphrases\\\\n\\\\nAn agent that calls `/spec`, then `/plan`, then `/build`, etc. on the user's behalf.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Loses the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work\\\\n- Each hand-off summarizes context — accumulated drift over a long pipeline\\\\n- Doubles token cost: orchestrator turn + sub-agent turn for every step\\\\n- Removes user agency at exactly the points where judgment matters most\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the user as the orchestrator. Document the recommended sequence in `README.md` and let users invoke it.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### D. Deep persona trees\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` calls a `pre-ship-coordinator` that calls a `quality-coordinator` that calls `code-reviewer`.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Each layer adds latency and tokens with no decision value\\\\n- Debugging becomes a multi-level investigation\\\\n- The leaf personas lose context to multiple summarization steps\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the orchestration depth at most 1 (slash command → personas). The merge happens in the main agent.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Decision flow\\\\n\\\\nWhen considering a new orchestrated workflow, walk this flow:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nIs the work one perspective on one artifact?\\\\n├── Yes → Direct invocation. Stop.\\\\n└── No  → Will the same composition repeat?\\\\n         ├── No  → Direct invocation, ad hoc. Stop.\\\\n         └── Yes → Are sub-tasks independent?\\\\n                  ├── No  → Sequential slash commands run by user (Pattern 4).\\\\n                  └── Yes → Parallel fan-out with merge (Pattern 3).\\\\n                           Validate against the checklist above.\\\\n                           If any check fails → fall back to single-persona command (Pattern 2).\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## When to add a new pattern to this catalog\\\\n\\\\nAdd a new entry only after:\\\\n\\\\n1. You've used the pattern at least twice in real work\\\\n2. You can name a concrete artifact in this repo that demonstrates it\\\\n3. You can explain why an existing pattern wouldn't have worked\\\\n4. You can describe its anti-pattern shadow (what people will mistakenly build instead)\\\\n\\\\nPremature catalog entries become aspirational documentation that no one follows.\\\\n\\\",\\n The slash command is just a saved prompt.\\\\n\\\\n**Anti-signal:** if the slash command's body is mostly \\\\\\\"decide which persona to call,\\\\\\\" delete it and let the user call the persona directly.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 3. Parallel fan-out with merge\\\\n\\\\nMultiple personas operate on the same input concurrently, each producing an independent report. A merge step (in the main agent's context) synthesizes them into a single decision.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n                    ┌─→ code-reviewer    ─┐\\\\n/ship → fan out  ───┼─→ security-auditor ─┤→ merge → go/no-go + rollback\\\\n                    └─→ test-engineer    ─┘\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\n- The sub-tasks are genuinely independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering dependency)\\\\n- Each sub-agent benefits from its own context window\\\\n- The merge step is small enough to stay in the main context\\\\n- Wall-clock latency matters\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/ship`.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** N parallel sub-agent contexts + one merge turn. Higher than direct invocation, but faster wall-clock and produces better reports because each sub-agent stays focused on its single perspective.\\\\n\\\\n**Validation checklist before adopting this pattern:**\\\\n- [ ] Can I run all sub-agents at the same time without ordering issues?\\\\n- [ ] Does each persona produce a different *kind* of finding, not just the same finding from a different angle?\\\\n- [ ] Will the merge step fit in the main agent's remaining context?\\\\n- [ ] Is the user's wait time long enough that parallelism is actually noticeable?\\\\n\\\\nIf any answer is \\\\\\\"no,\\\\\\\" fall back to direct invocation or a single-persona command.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 4. Sequential pipeline as user-driven slash commands\\\\n\\\\nThe user runs slash commands in a defined order, carrying context (or commit history) between them. There is no orchestrator agent — the user IS the orchestrator.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nuser runs:  /spec  →  /plan  →  /build  →  /test  →  /review  →  /ship\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the workflow has dependencies (each step needs the previous step's output) and human judgment between steps adds value.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** the entire DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP lifecycle.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one sub-agent context per step. Free for the orchestration layer because there is no orchestrator agent.\\\\n\\\\n**Why not automate it:** an LLM \\\\\\\"lifecycle orchestrator\\\\\\\" would (a) lose nuance between steps because it has to summarize for hand-off, (b) skip the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work early, and (c) double the token cost via paraphrasing turns.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 5. Research isolation (context preservation)\\\\n\\\\nWhen a task requires reading large amounts of material that shouldn't pollute the main context, spawn a research sub-agent that returns only a digest.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nmain agent → research sub-agent (reads 50 files) → digest → main agent continues\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\n- The main session needs to stay focused on a downstream task\\\\n- The investigation result is much smaller than the input it consumes\\\\n- The decision quality benefits from the main agent having room to think after\\\\n\\\\n**Examples:** \\\\\\\"Find every call site of this deprecated API across the monorepo,\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\"Summarize what these 30 ADRs say about caching.\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one isolated sub-agent context. Worth it any time the alternative is loading hundreds of files into the main context.\\\\n\\\\n**On Claude Code, use the built-in `Explore` subagent** rather than defining a custom research persona. `Explore` runs on Haiku, is denied write/edit tools, and is purpose-built for this pattern. Define a custom research subagent only when `Explore` doesn't fit (e.g. you need a domain-specific system prompt the model wouldn't infer).\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Claude Code compatibility\\\\n\\\\nThis catalog is harness-agnostic, but most readers will run it on Claude Code. Here's how each pattern maps onto Claude Code's primitives — and where the platform enforces our rules for us.\\\\n\\\\n### Where personas live\\\\n\\\\nPlugin subagents go in `agents/` at the plugin root. This repo is a plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), so `agents/code-reviewer.md`, `agents/security-auditor.md`, and `agents/test-engineer.md` are auto-discovered when the plugin is enabled. No path configuration needed.\\\\n\\\\n### Subagents vs. Agent Teams\\\\n\\\\nClaude Code has two parallelism primitives. Pattern 3 (parallel fan-out with merge) maps to **subagents**. If you need teammates that talk to each other, use **Agent Teams** instead.\\\\n\\\\n| | Subagents | Agent Teams |\\\\n|--|-----------|-------------|\\\\n| Coordination | Main agent fans out, sub-agents only report back | Teammates message each other, share a task list |\\\\n| Context | Own context window per subagent | Own context window per teammate |\\\\n| When to use | Independent tasks producing reports | Collaborative work needing discussion |\\\\n| Status | Stable | Experimental — requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` |\\\\n| Cost | Lower | Higher — each teammate is a separate Claude instance |\\\\n\\\\n**The personas in this repo work in both modes.** When spawned as subagents (e.g. by `/ship`), they report findings to the main session. When spawned as teammates (`Spawn a teammate using the security-auditor agent type…`), they can challenge each other's findings directly. The persona definition is the same; only the spawning context changes.\\\\n\\\\nOne subtlety: the `skills` and `mcpServers` frontmatter fields in a persona are honored when it runs as a subagent but **ignored when it runs as a teammate** — teammates load skills and MCP servers from your project and user settings, the same as a regular session. If a persona depends on a specific skill or MCP server being loaded, configure it at the session level so it's available in both modes.\\\\n\\\\n### Platform-enforced rules\\\\n\\\\nTwo rules in this catalog aren't just convention — Claude Code enforces them:\\\\n\\\\n- **\\\\\\\"Subagents cannot spawn other subagents\\\\\\\"** (verbatim from the docs). Anti-pattern B (persona-calls-persona) and Anti-pattern D (deep persona trees) cannot exist on Claude Code by construction.\\\\n- **\\\\\\\"No nested teams\\\\\\\"** — teammates cannot spawn their own teams. Same anti-patterns blocked at the team level.\\\\n\\\\nThis means you can adopt the patterns in this catalog without worrying about contributors accidentally building the anti-patterns. They'll just fail to load.\\\\n\\\\n### Built-in subagents to know about\\\\n\\\\nBefore defining a custom subagent, check whether one of these covers the role:\\\\n\\\\n| Built-in | Purpose |\\\\n|----------|---------|\\\\n| `Explore` | Read-only codebase search and analysis. Use this for Pattern 5 (research isolation). |\\\\n| `Plan` | Read-only research during plan mode. |\\\\n| `general-purpose` | Multi-step tasks needing both exploration and modification. |\\\\n\\\\nDon't redefine these. Layer your specialist personas (code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-engineer) on top of them.\\\\n\\\\n### Frontmatter restrictions for plugin agents\\\\n\\\\nPlugin subagents do **not** support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields — these are silently ignored. If a future persona needs any of those, the user must copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` instead.\\\\n\\\\nThe fields that DO work in plugin agents are: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation`, `color`, `initialPrompt`. Use `model` per-persona if you want to optimize cost (e.g. Haiku for `test-engineer` coverage scans, Sonnet for `code-reviewer`, Opus for `security-auditor`).\\\\n\\\\n### Spawning multiple subagents in parallel\\\\n\\\\nIn Claude Code, parallel fan-out (Pattern 3) requires issuing **multiple Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn**. Sequential turns serialize execution. `/ship` calls this out explicitly. Any new orchestrator command should do the same.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Worked example: Agent Teams for competing-hypothesis debugging\\\\n\\\\nThis example shows when to reach for **Agent Teams** instead of `/ship`'s subagent fan-out. The two patterns look similar from a distance — both spawn the same three personas — but the value comes from a different place.\\\\n\\\\n### The scenario\\\\n\\\\n> *Checkout occasionally hangs for ~30 seconds before completing. It happens roughly once every 50 sessions. No errors in logs. Started after last week's release.*\\\\n\\\\nPlausible root causes (mutually exclusive, all fit the symptoms):\\\\n\\\\n1. A race condition in the new payment-confirmation flow\\\\n2. An auth check that occasionally falls through to a slow synchronous network call\\\\n3. A missing index on a query that scales with cart size\\\\n4. A flaky third-party API where the SDK retries silently before timing out\\\\n\\\\nA single agent will pick the first plausible theory and stop investigating. A `/ship`-style subagent fan-out would have each persona report independently — but their reports never meet, so nothing rules out the wrong theories.\\\\n\\\\nThis is exactly the case the Agent Teams docs describe: *\\\\\\\"With multiple independent investigators actively trying to disprove each other, the theory that survives is much more likely to be the actual root cause.\\\\\\\"*\\\\n\\\\n### Why this is *not* a `/ship` job\\\\n\\\\n| | `/ship` (subagents) | Agent Teams |\\\\n|--|--------------------|-------------|\\\\n| Sub-agents see | The same diff, different lenses | A shared task list, each other's messages |\\\\n| Output | Three independent reports → one merge | Adversarial debate → consensus root cause |\\\\n| Right when | You want a verdict on a known artifact | You want to *find* the artifact among hypotheses |\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` is a verdict; Agent Teams is an investigation.\\\\n\\\\n### Setup (one-time, per-environment)\\\\n\\\\nAgent Teams is experimental. In `~/.claude/settings.json`:\\\\n\\\\n```json\\\\n{\\\\n  \\\\\\\"env\\\\\\\": {\\\\n    \\\\\\\"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"1\\\\\\\"\\\\n  }\\\\n}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nRequires Claude Code v2.1.32 or later. The personas in this repo are picked up automatically — no team-config files to author by hand.\\\\n\\\\n### The trigger prompt\\\\n\\\\nType into the lead session, in natural language:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nUsers report checkout hangs for ~30 seconds intermittently after last\\\\nweek's release. No errors in logs.\\\\n\\\\nCreate an agent team to debug this with competing hypotheses. Spawn\\\\nthree teammates using the existing agent types:\\\\n\\\\n  - code-reviewer  — investigate race conditions and blocking calls\\\\n                     in the checkout code path\\\\n  - security-auditor — investigate auth checks, session handling,\\\\n                       and any synchronous network calls added recently\\\\n  - test-engineer  — propose tests that would distinguish between the\\\\n                     hypotheses and check coverage gaps in checkout\\\\n\\\\nHave them message each other directly to challenge each other's\\\\ntheories. Update findings as consensus emerges. Only converge when\\\\ntwo teammates agree they can disprove the others'.\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe lead spawns three teammates referencing the existing persona names. The persona body is **appended** to each teammate's system prompt as additional instructions (on top of the team-coordination instructions the lead installs); the trigger prompt above becomes their task.\\\\n\\\\n### What happens\\\\n\\\\n1. Each teammate runs in its own context window, exploring the codebase from its own lens.\\\\n2. Teammates use `message` to send findings to each other directly. The lead doesn't have to relay.\\\\n3. The shared task list shows who's investigating what — visible at any time with `Ctrl+T` (in-process mode) or in a tmux pane (split mode).\\\\n4. When `code-reviewer` finds a `Promise.all` that should be sequential, it messages `security-auditor` to confirm the auth call isn't part of the race. `security-auditor` checks and replies — either confirming the race is the real issue or producing counter-evidence.\\\\n5. `test-engineer` proposes a focused integration test for whichever theory is winning, which the team uses to verify before declaring consensus.\\\\n6. The lead synthesizes the converged finding and presents it to you.\\\\n\\\\nYou can interrupt at any teammate by cycling with `Shift+Down` and typing — useful for redirecting an investigator who's gone down a wrong path.\\\\n\\\\n### When to clean up\\\\n\\\\nWhen the investigation lands on a root cause, tell the lead:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nClean up the team\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAlways cleanup through the lead, not a teammate (per the docs: teammates lack full team context for cleanup).\\\\n\\\\n### Cost expectation\\\\n\\\\nThree Sonnet teammates running for ~10–15 minutes of investigation costs noticeably more than the same three personas spawned as subagents by `/ship`. The justification is *quality of conclusion* — for production debugging where the wrong fix is expensive, the extra tokens are a bargain. For a routine PR review, stick with `/ship`.\\\\n\\\\n### Anti-pattern in this scenario\\\\n\\\\nDo **not** rebuild this as a `/debug` slash command that fans out subagents. Subagents can't message each other — you'd lose the adversarial debate that makes the pattern work. If a workflow keeps coming up, document the trigger prompt above as a snippet rather than wrapping it in a slash command that misuses subagents.\\\\n\\\\n### When *not* to use Agent Teams\\\\n\\\\n- Production-bound verdict on a known diff → use `/ship` (subagents).\\\\n- One specialist perspective on one artifact → direct persona invocation.\\\\n- Sequential lifecycle (spec → plan → build) → user-driven slash commands (Pattern 4).\\\\n- Read-heavy research with a small digest → built-in `Explore` subagent.\\\\n\\\\nReach for Agent Teams only when teammates **need** to challenge each other to produce the right answer.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Anti-patterns\\\\n\\\\n### A. Router persona (\\\\\\\"meta-orchestrator\\\\\\\")\\\\n\\\\nA persona whose job is to decide which other persona to call.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n/work → router-persona → \\\\\\\"this needs a review\\\\\\\" → code-reviewer → router (paraphrases) → user\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\\\\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + roughly 2× token cost\\\\n- The user already knew they wanted a review; they could have called `/review` directly\\\\n- Replicates the work that slash commands and intent mapping in `AGENTS.md` already do\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** add or refine slash commands. Document intent → command mapping in `AGENTS.md`.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### B. Persona that calls another persona\\\\n\\\\nA `code-reviewer` that internally invokes `security-auditor` when it sees auth code.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Personas were designed to produce a single perspective; chaining them defeats that\\\\n- The summary the calling persona passes loses context the called persona needs\\\\n- Failure modes multiply (which persona's output format wins? whose rules apply?)\\\\n- Hides cost from the user\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** have the calling persona *recommend* a follow-up audit in its report. The user or a slash command runs the second pass.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### C. Sequential orchestrator that paraphrases\\\\n\\\\nAn agent that calls `/spec`, then `/plan`, then `/build`, etc. on the user's behalf.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Loses the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work\\\\n- Each hand-off summarizes context — accumulated drift over a long pipeline\\\\n- Doubles token cost: orchestrator turn + sub-agent turn for every step\\\\n- Removes user agency at exactly the points where judgment matters most\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the user as the orchestrator. Document the recommended sequence in `README.md` and let users invoke it.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### D. Deep persona trees\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` calls a `pre-ship-coordinator` that calls a `quality-coordinator` that calls `code-reviewer`.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Each layer adds latency and tokens with no decision value\\\\n- Debugging becomes a multi-level investigation\\\\n- The leaf personas lose context to multiple summarization steps\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the orchestration depth at most 1 (slash command → personas). The merge happens in the main agent.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Decision flow\\\\n\\\\nWhen considering a new orchestrated workflow, walk this flow:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nIs the work one perspective on one artifact?\\\\n├── Yes → Direct invocation. Stop.\\\\n└── No  → Will the same composition repeat?\\\\n         ├── No  → Direct invocation, ad hoc. Stop.\\\\n         └── Yes → Are sub-tasks independent?\\\\n                  ├── No  → Sequential slash commands run by user (Pattern 4).\\\\n                  └── Yes → Parallel fan-out with merge (Pattern 3).\\\\n                           Validate against the checklist above.\\\\n                           If any check fails → fall back to single-persona command (Pattern 2).\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## When to add a new pattern to this catalog\\\\n\\\\nAdd a new entry only after:\\\\n\\\\n1. You've used the pattern at least twice in real work\\\\n2. You can name a concrete artifact in this repo that demonstrates it\\\\n3. You can explain why an existing pattern wouldn't have worked\\\\n4. You can describe its anti-pattern shadow (what people will mistakenly build instead)\\\\n\\\\nPremature catalog entries become aspirational documentation that no one follows.\\\\n\\\",\\n Read this before adding a new slash command that coordinates multiple personas, or before introducing a new persona that \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"wraps\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" existing ones.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe governing rule: **the user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. Personas do not invoke other personas.** Skills are mandatory hops inside a persona's workflow.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Endorsed patterns\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### 1. Direct invocation (no orchestration)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nSingle persona, single perspective, single artifact. The default and the cheapest option.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nuser → code-reviewer → report → user\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Use when:** the work is one perspective on one artifact and you can describe it in one sentence.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Examples:**\\\\\\\\n- \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Review this PR\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" → `code-reviewer`\\\\\\\\n- \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Find security issues in `auth.ts`\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" → `security-auditor`\\\\\\\\n- \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"What tests are missing for the checkout flow?\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" → `test-engineer`\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Cost:** one round trip. The baseline you should always compare orchestrated patterns against.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### 2. Single-persona slash command\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA slash command that wraps one persona with the project's skills. Saves the user from re-explaining the workflow every time.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n/review → code-reviewer (with code-review-and-quality skill) → report\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Use when:** the same single-persona invocation happens repeatedly with the same setup.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/review`, `/test`, `/code-simplify`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Cost:** same as direct invocation. The slash command is just a saved prompt.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Anti-signal:** if the slash command's body is mostly \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"decide which persona to call,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" delete it and let the user call the persona directly.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### 3. Parallel fan-out with merge\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nMultiple personas operate on the same input concurrently, each producing an independent report. A merge step (in the main agent's context) synthesizes them into a single decision.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n                    ┌─→ code-reviewer    ─┐\\\\\\\\n/ship → fan out  ───┼─→ security-auditor ─┤→ merge → go/no-go + rollback\\\\\\\\n                    └─→ test-engineer    ─┘\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\\\\\n- The sub-tasks are genuinely independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering dependency)\\\\\\\\n- Each sub-agent benefits from its own context window\\\\\\\\n- The merge step is small enough to stay in the main context\\\\\\\\n- Wall-clock latency matters\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/ship`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Cost:** N parallel sub-agent contexts + one merge turn. Higher than direct invocation, but faster wall-clock and produces better reports because each sub-agent stays focused on its single perspective.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Validation checklist before adopting this pattern:**\\\\\\\\n- [ ] Can I run all sub-agents at the same time without ordering issues?\\\\\\\\n- [ ] Does each persona produce a different *kind* of finding, not just the same finding from a different angle?\\\\\\\\n- [ ] Will the merge step fit in the main agent's remaining context?\\\\\\\\n- [ ] Is the user's wait time long enough that parallelism is actually noticeable?\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nIf any answer is \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"no,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" fall back to direct invocation or a single-persona command.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### 4. Sequential pipeline as user-driven slash commands\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe user runs slash commands in a defined order, carrying context (or commit history) between them. There is no orchestrator agent — the user IS the orchestrator.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nuser runs:  /spec  →  /plan  →  /build  →  /test  →  /review  →  /ship\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Use when:** the workflow has dependencies (each step needs the previous step's output) and human judgment between steps adds value.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** the entire DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP lifecycle.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Cost:** one sub-agent context per step. Free for the orchestration layer because there is no orchestrator agent.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why not automate it:** an LLM \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"lifecycle orchestrator\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" would (a) lose nuance between steps because it has to summarize for hand-off, (b) skip the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work early, and (c) double the token cost via paraphrasing turns.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### 5. Research isolation (context preservation)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nWhen a task requires reading large amounts of material that shouldn't pollute the main context, spawn a research sub-agent that returns only a digest.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nmain agent → research sub-agent (reads 50 files) → digest → main agent continues\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\\\\\n- The main session needs to stay focused on a downstream task\\\\\\\\n- The investigation result is much smaller than the input it consumes\\\\\\\\n- The decision quality benefits from the main agent having room to think after\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Examples:** \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Find every call site of this deprecated API across the monorepo,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Summarize what these 30 ADRs say about caching.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Cost:** one isolated sub-agent context. Worth it any time the alternative is loading hundreds of files into the main context.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**On Claude Code, use the built-in `Explore` subagent** rather than defining a custom research persona. `Explore` runs on Haiku, is denied write/edit tools, and is purpose-built for this pattern. Define a custom research subagent only when `Explore` doesn't fit (e.g. you need a domain-specific system prompt the model wouldn't infer).\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Claude Code compatibility\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis catalog is harness-agnostic, but most readers will run it on Claude Code. Here's how each pattern maps onto Claude Code's primitives — and where the platform enforces our rules for us.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Where personas live\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPlugin subagents go in `agents/` at the plugin root. This repo is a plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), so `agents/code-reviewer.md`, `agents/security-auditor.md`, and `agents/test-engineer.md` are auto-discovered when the plugin is enabled. No path configuration needed.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Subagents vs. Agent Teams\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nClaude Code has two parallelism primitives. Pattern 3 (parallel fan-out with merge) maps to **subagents**. If you need teammates that talk to each other, use **Agent Teams** instead.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n| | Subagents | Agent Teams |\\\\\\\\n|--|-----------|-------------|\\\\\\\\n| Coordination | Main agent fans out, sub-agents only report back | Teammates message each other, share a task list |\\\\\\\\n| Context | Own context window per subagent | Own context window per teammate |\\\\\\\\n| When to use | Independent tasks producing reports | Collaborative work needing discussion |\\\\\\\\n| Status | Stable | Experimental — requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` |\\\\\\\\n| Cost | Lower | Higher — each teammate is a separate Claude instance |\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**The personas in this repo work in both modes.** When spawned as subagents (e.g. by `/ship`), they report findings to the main session. When spawned as teammates (`Spawn a teammate using the security-auditor agent type…`), they can challenge each other's findings directly. The persona definition is the same; only the spawning context changes.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nOne subtlety: the `skills` and `mcpServers` frontmatter fields in a persona are honored when it runs as a subagent but **ignored when it runs as a teammate** — teammates load skills and MCP servers from your project and user settings, the same as a regular session. If a persona depends on a specific skill or MCP server being loaded, configure it at the session level so it's available in both modes.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Platform-enforced rules\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nTwo rules in this catalog aren't just convention — Claude Code enforces them:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- **\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Subagents cannot spawn other subagents\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"** (verbatim from the docs). Anti-pattern B (persona-calls-persona) and Anti-pattern D (deep persona trees) cannot exist on Claude Code by construction.\\\\\\\\n- **\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"No nested teams\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"** — teammates cannot spawn their own teams. Same anti-patterns blocked at the team level.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis means you can adopt the patterns in this catalog without worrying about contributors accidentally building the anti-patterns. They'll just fail to load.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Built-in subagents to know about\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nBefore defining a custom subagent, check whether one of these covers the role:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n| Built-in | Purpose |\\\\\\\\n|----------|---------|\\\\\\\\n| `Explore` | Read-only codebase search and analysis. Use this for Pattern 5 (research isolation). |\\\\\\\\n| `Plan` | Read-only research during plan mode. |\\\\\\\\n| `general-purpose` | Multi-step tasks needing both exploration and modification. |\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nDon't redefine these. Layer your specialist personas (code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-engineer) on top of them.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Frontmatter restrictions for plugin agents\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPlugin subagents do **not** support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields — these are silently ignored. If a future persona needs any of those, the user must copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` instead.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe fields that DO work in plugin agents are: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation`, `color`, `initialPrompt`. Use `model` per-persona if you want to optimize cost (e.g. Haiku for `test-engineer` coverage scans, Sonnet for `code-reviewer`, Opus for `security-auditor`).\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Spawning multiple subagents in parallel\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nIn Claude Code, parallel fan-out (Pattern 3) requires issuing **multiple Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn**. Sequential turns serialize execution. `/ship` calls this out explicitly. Any new orchestrator command should do the same.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Worked example: Agent Teams for competing-hypothesis debugging\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis example shows when to reach for **Agent Teams** instead of `/ship`'s subagent fan-out. The two patterns look similar from a distance — both spawn the same three personas — but the value comes from a different place.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### The scenario\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n> *Checkout occasionally hangs for ~30 seconds before completing. It happens roughly once every 50 sessions. No errors in logs. Started after last week's release.*\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPlausible root causes (mutually exclusive, all fit the symptoms):\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. A race condition in the new payment-confirmation flow\\\\\\\\n2. An auth check that occasionally falls through to a slow synchronous network call\\\\\\\\n3. A missing index on a query that scales with cart size\\\\\\\\n4. A flaky third-party API where the SDK retries silently before timing out\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA single agent will pick the first plausible theory and stop investigating. A `/ship`-style subagent fan-out would have each persona report independently — but their reports never meet, so nothing rules out the wrong theories.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis is exactly the case the Agent Teams docs describe: *\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"With multiple independent investigators actively trying to disprove each other, the theory that survives is much more likely to be the actual root cause.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"*\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Why this is *not* a `/ship` job\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n| | `/ship` (subagents) | Agent Teams |\\\\\\\\n|--|--------------------|-------------|\\\\\\\\n| Sub-agents see | The same diff, different lenses | A shared task list, each other's messages |\\\\\\\\n| Output | Three independent reports → one merge | Adversarial debate → consensus root cause |\\\\\\\\n| Right when | You want a verdict on a known artifact | You want to *find* the artifact among hypotheses |\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n`/ship` is a verdict; Agent Teams is an investigation.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Setup (one-time, per-environment)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAgent Teams is experimental. In `~/.claude/settings.json`:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```json\\\\\\\\n{\\\\\\\\n  \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"env\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\": {\\\\\\\\n    \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"1\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n  }\\\\\\\\n}\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nRequires Claude Code v2.1.32 or later. The personas in this repo are picked up automatically — no team-config files to author by hand.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### The trigger prompt\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nType into the lead session, in natural language:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nUsers report checkout hangs for ~30 seconds intermittently after last\\\\\\\\nweek's release. No errors in logs.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nCreate an agent team to debug this with competing hypotheses. Spawn\\\\\\\\nthree teammates using the existing agent types:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n  - code-reviewer  — investigate race conditions and blocking calls\\\\\\\\n                     in the checkout code path\\\\\\\\n  - security-auditor — investigate auth checks, session handling,\\\\\\\\n                       and any synchronous network calls added recently\\\\\\\\n  - test-engineer  — propose tests that would distinguish between the\\\\\\\\n                     hypotheses and check coverage gaps in checkout\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nHave them message each other directly to challenge each other's\\\\\\\\ntheories. Update findings as consensus emerges. Only converge when\\\\\\\\ntwo teammates agree they can disprove the others'.\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe lead spawns three teammates referencing the existing persona names. The persona body is **appended** to each teammate's system prompt as additional instructions (on top of the team-coordination instructions the lead installs); the trigger prompt above becomes their task.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### What happens\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. Each teammate runs in its own context window, exploring the codebase from its own lens.\\\\\\\\n2. Teammates use `message` to send findings to each other directly. The lead doesn't have to relay.\\\\\\\\n3. The shared task list shows who's investigating what — visible at any time with `Ctrl+T` (in-process mode) or in a tmux pane (split mode).\\\\\\\\n4. When `code-reviewer` finds a `Promise.all` that should be sequential, it messages `security-auditor` to confirm the auth call isn't part of the race. `security-auditor` checks and replies — either confirming the race is the real issue or producing counter-evidence.\\\\\\\\n5. `test-engineer` proposes a focused integration test for whichever theory is winning, which the team uses to verify before declaring consensus.\\\\\\\\n6. The lead synthesizes the converged finding and presents it to you.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nYou can interrupt at any teammate by cycling with `Shift+Down` and typing — useful for redirecting an investigator who's gone down a wrong path.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### When to clean up\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nWhen the investigation lands on a root cause, tell the lead:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nClean up the team\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAlways cleanup through the lead, not a teammate (per the docs: teammates lack full team context for cleanup).\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Cost expectation\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThree Sonnet teammates running for ~10–15 minutes of investigation costs noticeably more than the same three personas spawned as subagents by `/ship`. The justification is *quality of conclusion* — for production debugging where the wrong fix is expensive, the extra tokens are a bargain. For a routine PR review, stick with `/ship`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Anti-pattern in this scenario\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nDo **not** rebuild this as a `/debug` slash command that fans out subagents. Subagents can't message each other — you'd lose the adversarial debate that makes the pattern work. If a workflow keeps coming up, document the trigger prompt above as a snippet rather than wrapping it in a slash command that misuses subagents.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### When *not* to use Agent Teams\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- Production-bound verdict on a known diff → use `/ship` (subagents).\\\\\\\\n- One specialist perspective on one artifact → direct persona invocation.\\\\\\\\n- Sequential lifecycle (spec → plan → build) → user-driven slash commands (Pattern 4).\\\\\\\\n- Read-heavy research with a small digest → built-in `Explore` subagent.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nReach for Agent Teams only when teammates **need** to challenge each other to produce the right answer.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Anti-patterns\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### A. Router persona (\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"meta-orchestrator\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\")\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA persona whose job is to decide which other persona to call.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n/work → router-persona → \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"this needs a review\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" → code-reviewer → router (paraphrases) → user\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\\\\\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\\\\\\\\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + roughly 2× token cost\\\\\\\\n- The user already knew they wanted a review; they could have called `/review` directly\\\\\\\\n- Replicates the work that slash commands and intent mapping in `AGENTS.md` already do\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**What to do instead:** add or refine slash commands. Document intent → command mapping in `AGENTS.md`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### B. Persona that calls another persona\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA `code-reviewer` that internally invokes `security-auditor` when it sees auth code.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\\\\\n- Personas were designed to produce a single perspective; chaining them defeats that\\\\\\\\n- The summary the calling persona passes loses context the called persona needs\\\\\\\\n- Failure modes multiply (which persona's output format wins? whose rules apply?)\\\\\\\\n- Hides cost from the user\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**What to do instead:** have the calling persona *recommend* a follow-up audit in its report. The user or a slash command runs the second pass.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### C. Sequential orchestrator that paraphrases\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAn agent that calls `/spec`, then `/plan`, then `/build`, etc. on the user's behalf.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\\\\\n- Loses the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work\\\\\\\\n- Each hand-off summarizes context — accumulated drift over a long pipeline\\\\\\\\n- Doubles token cost: orchestrator turn + sub-agent turn for every step\\\\\\\\n- Removes user agency at exactly the points where judgment matters most\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the user as the orchestrator. Document the recommended sequence in `README.md` and let users invoke it.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### D. Deep persona trees\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n`/ship` calls a `pre-ship-coordinator` that calls a `quality-coordinator` that calls `code-reviewer`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\\\\\n- Each layer adds latency and tokens with no decision value\\\\\\\\n- Debugging becomes a multi-level investigation\\\\\\\\n- The leaf personas lose context to multiple summarization steps\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the orchestration depth at most 1 (slash command → personas). The merge happens in the main agent.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Decision flow\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nWhen considering a new orchestrated workflow, walk this flow:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nIs the work one perspective on one artifact?\\\\\\\\n├── Yes → Direct invocation. Stop.\\\\\\\\n└── No  → Will the same composition repeat?\\\\\\\\n         ├── No  → Direct invocation, ad hoc. Stop.\\\\\\\\n         └── Yes → Are sub-tasks independent?\\\\\\\\n                  ├── No  → Sequential slash commands run by user (Pattern 4).\\\\\\\\n                  └── Yes → Parallel fan-out with merge (Pattern 3).\\\\\\\\n                           Validate against the checklist above.\\\\\\\\n                           If any check fails → fall back to single-persona command (Pattern 2).\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## When to add a new pattern to this catalog\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAdd a new entry only after:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. You've used the pattern at least twice in real work\\\\\\\\n2. You can name a concrete artifact in this repo that demonstrates it\\\\\\\\n3. You can explain why an existing pattern wouldn't have worked\\\\\\\\n4. You can describe its anti-pattern shadow (what people will mistakenly build instead)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPremature catalog entries become aspirational documentation that no one follows.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\",\\\\n  \\\\\\\"encoding\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"base64\\\\\\\",\\\\n  \\\\\\\"_links\\\\\\\": {\\\\n    \\\\\\\"self\\\\\\\":
