The slash command is just a saved prompt.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Anti-signal:** if the slash command's body is mostly \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"decide which persona to call,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" delete it and let the user call the persona directly.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### 3. Parallel fan-out with merge\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nMultiple personas operate on the same input concurrently, each producing an independent report. A merge step (in the main agent's context) synthesizes them into a single decision.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n                    ┌─→ code-reviewer    ─┐\\\\\\\\n/ship → fan out  ───┼─→ security-auditor ─┤→ merge → go/no-go + rollback\\\\\\\\n                    └─→ test-engineer    ─┘\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\\\\\n- The sub-tasks are genuinely independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering dependency)\\\\\\\\n- Each sub-agent benefits from its own context window\\\\\\\\n- The merge step is small enough to stay in the main context\\\\\\\\n- Wall-clock latency matters\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/ship`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Cost:** N parallel sub-agent contexts + one merge turn. Higher than direct invocation, but faster wall-clock and produces better reports because each sub-agent stays focused on its single perspective.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Validation checklist before adopting this pattern:**\\\\\\\\n- [ ] Can I run all sub-agents at the same time without ordering issues?\\\\\\\\n- [ ] Does each persona produce a different *kind* of finding, not just the same finding from a different angle?\\\\\\\\n- [ ] Will the merge step fit in the main agent's remaining context?\\\\\\\\n- [ ] Is the user's wait time long enough that parallelism is actually noticeable?\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nIf any answer is \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"no,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" fall back to direct invocation or a single-persona command.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### 4. Sequential pipeline as user-driven slash commands\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe user runs slash commands in a defined order, carrying context (or commit history) between them. There is no orchestrator agent — the user IS the orchestrator.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nuser runs:  /spec  →  /plan  →  /build  →  /test  →  /review  →  /ship\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Use when:** the workflow has dependencies (each step needs the previous step's output) and human judgment between steps adds value.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** the entire DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP lifecycle.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Cost:** one sub-agent context per step. Free for the orchestration layer because there is no orchestrator agent.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why not automate it:** an LLM \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"lifecycle orchestrator\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" would (a) lose nuance between steps because it has to summarize for hand-off, (b) skip the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work early, and (c) double the token cost via paraphrasing turns.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### 5. Research isolation (context preservation)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nWhen a task requires reading large amounts of material that shouldn't pollute the main context, spawn a research sub-agent that returns only a digest.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nmain agent → research sub-agent (reads 50 files) → digest → main agent continues\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\\\\\n- The main session needs to stay focused on a downstream task\\\\\\\\n- The investigation result is much smaller than the input it consumes\\\\\\\\n- The decision quality benefits from the main agent having room to think after\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Examples:** \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Find every call site of this deprecated API across the monorepo,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Summarize what these 30 ADRs say about caching.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Cost:** one isolated sub-agent context. Worth it any time the alternative is loading hundreds of files into the main context.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**On Claude Code, use the built-in `Explore` subagent** rather than defining a custom research persona. `Explore` runs on Haiku, is denied write/edit tools, and is purpose-built for this pattern. Define a custom research subagent only when `Explore` doesn't fit (e.g. you need a domain-specific system prompt the model wouldn't infer).\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Claude Code compatibility\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis catalog is harness-agnostic, but most readers will run it on Claude Code. Here's how each pattern maps onto Claude Code's primitives — and where the platform enforces our rules for us.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Where personas live\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPlugin subagents go in `agents/` at the plugin root. This repo is a plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), so `agents/code-reviewer.md`, `agents/security-auditor.md`, and `agents/test-engineer.md` are auto-discovered when the plugin is enabled. No path configuration needed.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Subagents vs. Agent Teams\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nClaude Code has two parallelism primitives. Pattern 3 (parallel fan-out with merge) maps to **subagents**. If you need teammates that talk to each other, use **Agent Teams** instead.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n| | Subagents | Agent Teams |\\\\\\\\n|--|-----------|-------------|\\\\\\\\n| Coordination | Main agent fans out, sub-agents only report back | Teammates message each other, share a task list |\\\\\\\\n| Context | Own context window per subagent | Own context window per teammate |\\\\\\\\n| When to use | Independent tasks producing reports | Collaborative work needing discussion |\\\\\\\\n| Status | Stable | Experimental — requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` |\\\\\\\\n| Cost | Lower | Higher — each teammate is a separate Claude instance |\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**The personas in this repo work in both modes.** When spawned as subagents (e.g. by `/ship`), they report findings to the main session. When spawned as teammates (`Spawn a teammate using the security-auditor agent type…`), they can challenge each other's findings directly. The persona definition is the same; only the spawning context changes.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nOne subtlety: the `skills` and `mcpServers` frontmatter fields in a persona are honored when it runs as a subagent but **ignored when it runs as a teammate** — teammates load skills and MCP servers from your project and user settings, the same as a regular session. If a persona depends on a specific skill or MCP server being loaded, configure it at the session level so it's available in both modes.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Platform-enforced rules\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nTwo rules in this catalog aren't just convention — Claude Code enforces them:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- **\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Subagents cannot spawn other subagents\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"** (verbatim from the docs). Anti-pattern B (persona-calls-persona) and Anti-pattern D (deep persona trees) cannot exist on Claude Code by construction.\\\\\\\\n- **\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"No nested teams\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"** — teammates cannot spawn their own teams. Same anti-patterns blocked at the team level.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis means you can adopt the patterns in this catalog without worrying about contributors accidentally building the anti-patterns. They'll just fail to load.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Built-in subagents to know about\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nBefore defining a custom subagent, check whether one of these covers the role:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n| Built-in | Purpose |\\\\\\\\n|----------|---------|\\\\\\\\n| `Explore` | Read-only codebase search and analysis. Use this for Pattern 5 (research isolation). |\\\\\\\\n| `Plan` | Read-only research during plan mode. |\\\\\\\\n| `general-purpose` | Multi-step tasks needing both exploration and modification. |\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nDon't redefine these. Layer your specialist personas (code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-engineer) on top of them.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Frontmatter restrictions for plugin agents\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPlugin subagents do **not** support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields — these are silently ignored. If a future persona needs any of those, the user must copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` instead.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe fields that DO work in plugin agents are: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation`, `color`, `initialPrompt`. Use `model` per-persona if you want to optimize cost (e.g. Haiku for `test-engineer` coverage scans, Sonnet for `code-reviewer`, Opus for `security-auditor`).\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Spawning multiple subagents in parallel\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nIn Claude Code, parallel fan-out (Pattern 3) requires issuing **multiple Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn**. Sequential turns serialize execution. `/ship` calls this out explicitly. Any new orchestrator command should do the same.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Worked example: Agent Teams for competing-hypothesis debugging\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis example shows when to reach for **Agent Teams** instead of `/ship`'s subagent fan-out. The two patterns look similar from a distance — both spawn the same three personas — but the value comes from a different place.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### The scenario\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n> *Checkout occasionally hangs for ~30 seconds before completing. It happens roughly once every 50 sessions. No errors in logs. Started after last week's release.*\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPlausible root causes (mutually exclusive, all fit the symptoms):\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. A race condition in the new payment-confirmation flow\\\\\\\\n2. An auth check that occasionally falls through to a slow synchronous network call\\\\\\\\n3. A missing index on a query that scales with cart size\\\\\\\\n4. A flaky third-party API where the SDK retries silently before timing out\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA single agent will pick the first plausible theory and stop investigating. A `/ship`-style subagent fan-out would have each persona report independently — but their reports never meet, so nothing rules out the wrong theories.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis is exactly the case the Agent Teams docs describe: *\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"With multiple independent investigators actively trying to disprove each other, the theory that survives is much more likely to be the actual root cause.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"*\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Why this is *not* a `/ship` job\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n| | `/ship` (subagents) | Agent Teams |\\\\\\\\n|--|--------------------|-------------|\\\\\\\\n| Sub-agents see | The same diff, different lenses | A shared task list, each other's messages |\\\\\\\\n| Output | Three independent reports → one merge | Adversarial debate → consensus root cause |\\\\\\\\n| Right when | You want a verdict on a known artifact | You want to *find* the artifact among hypotheses |\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n`/ship` is a verdict; Agent Teams is an investigation.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Setup (one-time, per-environment)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAgent Teams is experimental. In `~/.claude/settings.json`:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```json\\\\\\\\n{\\\\\\\\n  \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"env\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\": {\\\\\\\\n    \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"1\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n  }\\\\\\\\n}\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nRequires Claude Code v2.1.32 or later. The personas in this repo are picked up automatically — no team-config files to author by hand.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### The trigger prompt\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nType into the lead session, in natural language:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nUsers report checkout hangs for ~30 seconds intermittently after last\\\\\\\\nweek's release. No errors in logs.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nCreate an agent team to debug this with competing hypotheses. Spawn\\\\\\\\nthree teammates using the existing agent types:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n  - code-reviewer  — investigate race conditions and blocking calls\\\\\\\\n                     in the checkout code path\\\\\\\\n  - security-auditor — investigate auth checks, session handling,\\\\\\\\n                       and any synchronous network calls added recently\\\\\\\\n  - test-engineer  — propose tests that would distinguish between the\\\\\\\\n                     hypotheses and check coverage gaps in checkout\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nHave them message each other directly to challenge each other's\\\\\\\\ntheories. Update findings as consensus emerges. Only converge when\\\\\\\\ntwo teammates agree they can disprove the others'.\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe lead spawns three teammates referencing the existing persona names. The persona body is **appended** to each teammate's system prompt as additional instructions (on top of the team-coordination instructions the lead installs); the trigger prompt above becomes their task.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### What happens\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. Each teammate runs in its own context window, exploring the codebase from its own lens.\\\\\\\\n2. Teammates use `message` to send findings to each other directly. The lead doesn't have to relay.\\\\\\\\n3. The shared task list shows who's investigating what — visible at any time with `Ctrl+T` (in-process mode) or in a tmux pane (split mode).\\\\\\\\n4. When `code-reviewer` finds a `Promise.all` that should be sequential, it messages `security-auditor` to confirm the auth call isn't part of the race. `security-auditor` checks and replies — either confirming the race is the real issue or producing counter-evidence.\\\\\\\\n5. `test-engineer` proposes a focused integration test for whichever theory is winning, which the team uses to verify before declaring consensus.\\\\\\\\n6. The lead synthesizes the converged finding and presents it to you.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nYou can interrupt at any teammate by cycling with `Shift+Down` and typing — useful for redirecting an investigator who's gone down a wrong path.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### When to clean up\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nWhen the investigation lands on a root cause, tell the lead:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nClean up the team\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAlways cleanup through the lead, not a teammate (per the docs: teammates lack full team context for cleanup).\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Cost expectation\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThree Sonnet teammates running for ~10–15 minutes of investigation costs noticeably more than the same three personas spawned as subagents by `/ship`. The justification is *quality of conclusion* — for production debugging where the wrong fix is expensive, the extra tokens are a bargain. For a routine PR review, stick with `/ship`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Anti-pattern in this scenario\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nDo **not** rebuild this as a `/debug` slash command that fans out subagents. Subagents can't message each other — you'd lose the adversarial debate that makes the pattern work. If a workflow keeps coming up, document the trigger prompt above as a snippet rather than wrapping it in a slash command that misuses subagents.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### When *not* to use Agent Teams\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- Production-bound verdict on a known diff → use `/ship` (subagents).\\\\\\\\n- One specialist perspective on one artifact → direct persona invocation.\\\\\\\\n- Sequential lifecycle (spec → plan → build) → user-driven slash commands (Pattern 4).\\\\\\\\n- Read-heavy research with a small digest → built-in `Explore` subagent.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nReach for Agent Teams only when teammates **need** to challenge each other to produce the right answer.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Anti-patterns\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### A. Router persona (\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"meta-orchestrator\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\")\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA persona whose job is to decide which other persona to call.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n/work → router-persona → \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"this needs a review\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" → code-reviewer → router (paraphrases) → user\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\\\\\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\\\\\\\\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + roughly 2× token cost\\\\\\\\n- The user already knew they wanted a review; they could have called `/review` directly\\\\\\\\n- Replicates the work that slash commands and intent mapping in `AGENTS.md` already do\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**What to do instead:** add or refine slash commands. Document intent → command mapping in `AGENTS.md`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### B. Persona that calls another persona\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA `code-reviewer` that internally invokes `security-auditor` when it sees auth code.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\\\\\n- Personas were designed to produce a single perspective; chaining them defeats that\\\\\\\\n- The summary the calling persona passes loses context the called persona needs\\\\\\\\n- Failure modes multiply (which persona's output format wins? whose rules apply?)\\\\\\\\n- Hides cost from the user\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**What to do instead:** have the calling persona *recommend* a follow-up audit in its report. The user or a slash command runs the second pass.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### C. Sequential orchestrator that paraphrases\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAn agent that calls `/spec`, then `/plan`, then `/build`, etc. on the user's behalf.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\\\\\n- Loses the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work\\\\\\\\n- Each hand-off summarizes context — accumulated drift over a long pipeline\\\\\\\\n- Doubles token cost: orchestrator turn + sub-agent turn for every step\\\\\\\\n- Removes user agency at exactly the points where judgment matters most\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the user as the orchestrator. Document the recommended sequence in `README.md` and let users invoke it.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### D. Deep persona trees\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n`/ship` calls a `pre-ship-coordinator` that calls a `quality-coordinator` that calls `code-reviewer`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\\\\\n- Each layer adds latency and tokens with no decision value\\\\\\\\n- Debugging becomes a multi-level investigation\\\\\\\\n- The leaf personas lose context to multiple summarization steps\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the orchestration depth at most 1 (slash command → personas). The merge happens in the main agent.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Decision flow\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nWhen considering a new orchestrated workflow, walk this flow:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nIs the work one perspective on one artifact?\\\\\\\\n├── Yes → Direct invocation. Stop.\\\\\\\\n└── No  → Will the same composition repeat?\\\\\\\\n         ├── No  → Direct invocation, ad hoc. Stop.\\\\\\\\n         └── Yes → Are sub-tasks independent?\\\\\\\\n                  ├── No  → Sequential slash commands run by user (Pattern 4).\\\\\\\\n                  └── Yes → Parallel fan-out with merge (Pattern 3).\\\\\\\\n                           Validate against the checklist above.\\\\\\\\n                           If any check fails → fall back to single-persona command (Pattern 2).\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## When to add a new pattern to this catalog\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nAdd a new entry only after:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. You've used the pattern at least twice in real work\\\\\\\\n2. You can name a concrete artifact in this repo that demonstrates it\\\\\\\\n3. You can explain why an existing pattern wouldn't have worked\\\\\\\\n4. You can describe its anti-pattern shadow (what people will mistakenly build instead)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPremature catalog entries become aspirational documentation that no one \\\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/main/references/orchestration-patterns.md\\\",\\n  \\\"type\\\": \\\"file\\\",\\n  \\\"content\\\": \\\"# Orchestration Patterns\\\\n\\\\nReference catalog of agent orchestration patterns this repo endorses, plus anti-patterns to avoid. Read this before adding a new slash command that coordinates multiple personas, or before introducing a new persona that \\\\\\\"wraps\\\\\\\" existing ones.\\\\n\\\\nThe governing rule: **the user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. Personas do not invoke other personas.** Skills are mandatory hops inside a persona's workflow.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Endorsed patterns\\\\n\\\\n### 1. Direct invocation (no orchestration)\\\\n\\\\nSingle persona, single perspective, single artifact. The default and the cheapest option.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nuser → code-reviewer → report → user\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the work is one perspective on one artifact and you can describe it in one sentence.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples:**\\\\n- \\\\\\\"Review this PR\\\\\\\" → `code-reviewer`\\\\n- \\\\\\\"Find security issues in `auth.ts`\\\\\\\" → `security-auditor`\\\\n- \\\\\\\"What tests are missing for the checkout flow?\\\\\\\" → `test-engineer`\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one round trip. The baseline you should always compare orchestrated patterns against.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 2. Single-persona slash command\\\\n\\\\nA slash command that wraps one persona with the project's skills. Saves the user from re-explaining the workflow every time.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n/review → code-reviewer (with code-review-and-quality skill) → report\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the same single-persona invocation happens repeatedly with the same setup.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/review`, `/test`, `/code-simplify`.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** same as direct invocation. The slash command is just a saved prompt.\\\\n\\\\n**Anti-signal:** if the slash command's body is mostly \\\\\\\"decide which persona to call,\\\\\\\" delete it and let the user call the persona directly.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 3. Parallel fan-out with merge\\\\n\\\\nMultiple personas operate on the same input concurrently, each producing an independent report. A merge step (in the main agent's context) synthesizes them into a single decision.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n                    ┌─→ code-reviewer    ─┐\\\\n/ship → fan out  ───┼─→ security-auditor ─┤→ merge → go/no-go + rollback\\\\n                    └─→ test-engineer    ─┘\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\n- The sub-tasks are genuinely independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering dependency)\\\\n- Each sub-agent benefits from its own context window\\\\n- The merge step is small enough to stay in the main context\\\\n- Wall-clock latency matters\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/ship`.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** N parallel sub-agent contexts + one merge turn. Higher than direct invocation, but faster wall-clock and produces better reports because each sub-agent stays focused on its single perspective.\\\\n\\\\n**Validation checklist before adopting this pattern:**\\\\n- [ ] Can I run all sub-agents at the same time without ordering issues?\\\\n- [ ] Does each persona produce a different *kind* of finding, not just the same finding from a different angle?\\\\n- [ ] Will the merge step fit in the main agent's remaining context?\\\\n- [ ] Is the user's wait time long enough that parallelism is actually noticeable?\\\\n\\\\nIf any answer is \\\\\\\"no,\\\\\\\" fall back to direct invocation or a single-persona command.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 4. Sequential pipeline as user-driven slash commands\\\\n\\\\nThe user runs slash commands in a defined order, carrying context (or commit history) between them. There is no orchestrator agent — the user IS the orchestrator.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nuser runs:  /spec  →  /plan  →  /build  →  /test  →  /review  →  /ship\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the workflow has dependencies (each step needs the previous step's output) and human judgment between steps adds value.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** the entire DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP lifecycle.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one sub-agent context per step. Free for the orchestration layer because there is no orchestrator agent.\\\\n\\\\n**Why not automate it:** an LLM \\\\\\\"lifecycle orchestrator\\\\\\\" would (a) lose nuance between steps because it has to summarize for hand-off, (b) skip the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work early, and (c) double the token cost via paraphrasing turns.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 5. Research isolation (context preservation)\\\\n\\\\nWhen a task requires reading large amounts of material that shouldn't pollute the main context, spawn a research sub-agent that returns only a digest.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nmain agent → research sub-agent (reads 50 files) → digest → main agent continues\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\n- The main session needs to stay focused on a downstream task\\\\n- The investigation result is much smaller than the input it consumes\\\\n- The decision quality benefits from the main agent having room to think after\\\\n\\\\n**Examples:** \\\\\\\"Find every call site of this deprecated API across the monorepo,\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\"Summarize what these 30 ADRs say about caching.\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one isolated sub-agent context. Worth it any time the alternative is loading hundreds of files into the main context.\\\\n\\\\n**On Claude Code, use the built-in `Explore` subagent** rather than defining a custom research persona. `Explore` runs on Haiku, is denied write/edit tools, and is purpose-built for this pattern. Define a custom research subagent only when `Explore` doesn't fit (e.g. you need a domain-specific system prompt the model wouldn't infer).\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Claude Code compatibility\\\\n\\\\nThis catalog is harness-agnostic, but most readers will run it on Claude Code. Here's how each pattern maps onto Claude Code's primitives — and where the platform enforces our rules for us.\\\\n\\\\n### Where personas live\\\\n\\\\nPlugin subagents go in `agents/` at the plugin root. This repo is a plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), so `agents/code-reviewer.md`, `agents/security-auditor.md`, and `agents/test-engineer.md` are auto-discovered when the plugin is enabled. No path configuration needed.\\\\n\\\\n### Subagents vs. Agent Teams\\\\n\\\\nClaude Code has two parallelism primitives. Pattern 3 (parallel fan-out with merge) maps to **subagents**. If you need teammates that talk to each other, use **Agent Teams** instead.\\\\n\\\\n| | Subagents | Agent Teams |\\\\n|--|-----------|-------------|\\\\n| Coordination | Main agent fans out, sub-agents only report back | Teammates message each other, share a task list |\\\\n| Context | Own context window per subagent | Own context window per teammate |\\\\n| When to use | Independent tasks producing reports | Collaborative work needing discussion |\\\\n| Status | Stable | Experimental — requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` |\\\\n| Cost | Lower | Higher — each teammate is a separate Claude instance |\\\\n\\\\n**The personas in this repo work in both modes.** When spawned as subagents (e.g. by `/ship`), they report findings to the main session. When spawned as teammates (`Spawn a teammate using the security-auditor agent type…`), they can challenge each other's findings directly. The persona definition is the same; only the spawning context changes.\\\\n\\\\nOne subtlety: the `skills` and `mcpServers` frontmatter fields in a persona are honored when it runs as a subagent but **ignored when it runs as a teammate** — teammates load skills and MCP servers from your project and user settings, the same as a regular session. If a persona depends on a specific skill or MCP server being loaded, configure it at the session level so it's available in both modes.\\\\n\\\\n### Platform-enforced rules\\\\n\\\\nTwo rules in this catalog aren't just convention — Claude Code enforces them:\\\\n\\\\n- **\\\\\\\"Subagents cannot spawn other subagents\\\\\\\"** (verbatim from the docs). Anti-pattern B (persona-calls-persona) and Anti-pattern D (deep persona trees) cannot exist on Claude Code by construction.\\\\n- **\\\\\\\"No nested teams\\\\\\\"** — teammates cannot spawn their own teams. Same anti-patterns blocked at the team level.\\\\n\\\\nThis means you can adopt the patterns in this catalog without worrying about contributors accidentally building the anti-patterns. They'll just fail to load.\\\\n\\\\n### Built-in subagents to know about\\\\n\\\\nBefore defining a custom subagent, check whether one of these covers the role:\\\\n\\\\n| Built-in | Purpose |\\\\n|----------|---------|\\\\n| `Explore` | Read-only codebase search and analysis. Use this for Pattern 5 (research isolation). |\\\\n| `Plan` | Read-only research during plan mode. |\\\\n| `general-purpose` | Multi-step tasks needing both exploration and modification. |\\\\n\\\\nDon't redefine these. Layer your specialist personas (code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-engineer) on top of them.\\\\n\\\\n### Frontmatter restrictions for plugin agents\\\\n\\\\nPlugin subagents do **not** support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields — these are silently ignored. If a future persona needs any of those, the user must copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` instead.\\\\n\\\\nThe fields that DO work in plugin agents are: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation`, `color`, `initialPrompt`. Use `model` per-persona if you want to optimize cost (e.g. Haiku for `test-engineer` coverage scans, Sonnet for `code-reviewer`, Opus for `security-auditor`).\\\\n\\\\n### Spawning multiple subagents in parallel\\\\n\\\\nIn Claude Code, parallel fan-out (Pattern 3) requires issuing **multiple Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn**. Sequential turns serialize execution. `/ship` calls this out explicitly. Any new orchestrator command should do the same.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Worked example: Agent Teams for competing-hypothesis debugging\\\\n\\\\nThis example shows when to reach for **Agent Teams** instead of `/ship`'s subagent fan-out. The two patterns look similar from a distance — both spawn the same three personas — but the value comes from a different place.\\\\n\\\\n### The scenario\\\\n\\\\n> *Checkout occasionally hangs for ~30 seconds before completing. It happens roughly once every 50 sessions. No errors in logs. Started after last week's release.*\\\\n\\\\nPlausible root causes (mutually exclusive, all fit the symptoms):\\\\n\\\\n1. A race condition in the new payment-confirmation flow\\\\n2. An auth check that occasionally falls through to a slow synchronous network call\\\\n3. A missing index on a query that scales with cart size\\\\n4. A flaky third-party API where the SDK retries silently before timing out\\\\n\\\\nA single agent will pick the first plausible theory and stop investigating. A `/ship`-style subagent fan-out would have each persona report independently — but their reports never meet, so nothing rules out the wrong theories.\\\\n\\\\nThis is exactly the case the Agent Teams docs describe: *\\\\\\\"With multiple independent investigators actively trying to disprove each other, the theory that survives is much more likely to be the actual root cause.\\\\\\\"*\\\\n\\\\n### Why this is *not* a `/ship` job\\\\n\\\\n| | `/ship` (subagents) | Agent Teams |\\\\n|--|--------------------|-------------|\\\\n| Sub-agents see | The same diff, different lenses | A shared task list, each other's messages |\\\\n| Output | Three independent reports → one merge | Adversarial debate → consensus root cause |\\\\n| Right when | You want a verdict on a known artifact | You want to *find* the artifact among hypotheses |\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` is a verdict; Agent Teams is an investigation.\\\\n\\\\n### Setup (one-time, per-environment)\\\\n\\\\nAgent Teams is experimental. In `~/.claude/settings.json`:\\\\n\\\\n```json\\\\n{\\\\n  \\\\\\\"env\\\\\\\": {\\\\n    \\\\\\\"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"1\\\\\\\"\\\\n  }\\\\n}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nRequires Claude Code v2.1.32 or later. The personas in this repo are picked up automatically — no team-config files to author by hand.\\\\n\\\\n### The trigger prompt\\\\n\\\\nType into the lead session, in natural language:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nUsers report checkout hangs for ~30 seconds intermittently after last\\\\nweek's release. No errors in logs.\\\\n\\\\nCreate an agent team to debug this with competing hypotheses. Spawn\\\\nthree teammates using the existing agent types:\\\\n\\\\n  - code-reviewer  — investigate race conditions and blocking calls\\\\n                     in the checkout code path\\\\n  - security-auditor — investigate auth checks, session handling,\\\\n                       and any synchronous network calls added recently\\\\n  - test-engineer  — propose tests that would distinguish between the\\\\n                     hypotheses and check coverage gaps in checkout\\\\n\\\\nHave them message each other directly to challenge each other's\\\\ntheories. Update findings as consensus emerges. Only converge when\\\\ntwo teammates agree they can disprove the others'.\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe lead spawns three teammates referencing the existing persona names. The persona body is **appended** to each teammate's system prompt as additional instructions (on top of the team-coordination instructions the lead installs); the trigger prompt above becomes their task.\\\\n\\\\n### What happens\\\\n\\\\n1. Each teammate runs in its own context window, exploring the codebase from its own lens.\\\\n2. Teammates use `message` to send findings to each other directly. The lead doesn't have to relay.\\\\n3. The shared task list shows who's investigating what — visible at any time with `Ctrl+T` (in-process mode) or in a tmux pane (split mode).\\\\n4. When `code-reviewer` finds a `Promise.all` that should be sequential, it messages `security-auditor` to confirm the auth call isn't part of the race. `security-auditor` checks and replies — either confirming the race is the real issue or producing counter-evidence.\\\\n5. `test-engineer` proposes a focused integration test for whichever theory is winning, which the team uses to verify before declaring consensus.\\\\n6. The lead synthesizes the converged finding and presents it to you.\\\\n\\\\nYou can interrupt at any teammate by cycling with `Shift+Down` and typing — useful for redirecting an investigator who's gone down a wrong path.\\\\n\\\\n### When to clean up\\\\n\\\\nWhen the investigation lands on a root cause, tell the lead:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nClean up the team\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAlways cleanup through the lead, not a teammate (per the docs: teammates lack full team context for cleanup).\\\\n\\\\n### Cost expectation\\\\n\\\\nThree Sonnet teammates running for ~10–15 minutes of investigation costs noticeably more than the same three personas spawned as subagents by `/ship`. The justification is *quality of conclusion* — for production debugging where the wrong fix is expensive, the extra tokens are a bargain. For a routine PR review, stick with `/ship`.\\\\n\\\\n### Anti-pattern in this scenario\\\\n\\\\nDo **not** rebuild this as a `/debug` slash command that fans out subagents. Subagents can't message each other — you'd lose the adversarial debate that makes the pattern work. If a workflow keeps coming up, document the trigger prompt above as a snippet rather than wrapping it in a slash command that misuses subagents.\\\\n\\\\n### When *not* to use Agent Teams\\\\n\\\\n- Production-bound verdict on a known diff → use `/ship` (subagents).\\\\n- One specialist perspective on one artifact → direct persona invocation.\\\\n- Sequential lifecycle (spec → plan → build) → user-driven slash commands (Pattern 4).\\\\n- Read-heavy research with a small digest → built-in `Explore` subagent.\\\\n\\\\nReach for Agent Teams only when teammates **need** to challenge each other to produce the right answer.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Anti-patterns\\\\n\\\\n### A. Router persona (\\\\\\\"meta-orchestrator\\\\\\\")\\\\n\\\\nA persona whose job is to decide which other persona to call.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n/work → router-persona → \\\\\\\"this needs a review\\\\\\\" → code-reviewer → router (paraphrases) → user\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\\\\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + roughly 2× token cost\\\\n- The user already knew they wanted a review; they could have called `/review` directly\\\\n- Replicates the work that slash commands and intent mapping in `AGENTS.md` already do\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** add or refine slash commands. Document intent → command mapping in `AGENTS.md`.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### B. Persona that calls another persona\\\\n\\\\nA `code-reviewer` that internally invokes `security-auditor` when it sees auth code.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Personas were designed to produce a single perspective; chaining them defeats that\\\\n- The summary the calling persona passes loses context the called persona needs\\\\n- Failure modes multiply (which persona's output format wins? whose rules apply?)\\\\n- Hides cost from the user\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** have the calling persona *recommend* a follow-up audit in its report. The user or a slash command runs the second pass.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### C. Sequential orchestrator that paraphrases\\\\n\\\\nAn agent that calls `/spec`, then `/plan`, then `/build`, etc. on the user's behalf.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Loses the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work\\\\n- Each hand-off summarizes context — accumulated drift over a long pipeline\\\\n- Doubles token cost: orchestrator turn + sub-agent turn for every step\\\\n- Removes user agency at exactly the points where judgment matters most\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the user as the orchestrator. Document the recommended sequence in `README.md` and let users invoke it.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### D. Deep persona trees\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` calls a `pre-ship-coordinator` that calls a `quality-coordinator` that calls `code-reviewer`.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Each layer adds latency and tokens with no decision value\\\\n- Debugging becomes a multi-level investigation\\\\n- The leaf personas lose context to multiple summarization steps\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the orchestration depth at most 1 (slash command → personas). The merge happens in the main agent.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Decision flow\\\\n\\\\nWhen considering a new orchestrated workflow, walk this flow:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nIs the work one perspective on one artifact?\\\\n├── Yes → Direct invocation. Stop.\\\\n└── No  → Will the same composition repeat?\\\\n         ├── No  → Direct invocation, ad hoc. Stop.\\\\n         └── Yes → Are sub-tasks independent?\\\\n                  ├── No  → Sequential slash commands run by user (Pattern 4).\\\\n                  └── Yes → Parallel fan-out with merge (Pattern 3).\\\\n                           Validate against the checklist above.\\\\n                           If any check fails → fall back to single-persona command (Pattern 2).\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## When to add a new pattern to this catalog\\\\n\\\\nAdd a new entry only after:\\\\n\\\\n1. You've used the pattern at least twice in real work\\\\n2. You can name a concrete artifact in this repo that demonstrates it\\\\n3. You can explain why an existing pattern wouldn't have worked\\\\n4. You can describe its anti-pattern shadow (what people will mistakenly build instead)\\\\n\\\\nPremature catalog entries become aspirational documentation that no one follows.\\\\n\\\",\\n agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Antigravity, etc.) when working with code in this repository.\\\\n\\\\n## Repository Overview\\\\n\\\\nA collection of skills for Claude.ai and Claude Code for senior software engineers. Skills are packaged instructions and scripts that extend Claude and your coding agents capabilities.\\\\n\\\\n## OpenCode Integration\\\\n\\\\nOpenCode uses a **skill-driven execution model** powered by the `skill` tool and this repository's `/skills` directory.\\\\n\\\\n### Core Rules\\\\n\\\\n- If a task matches a skill, you MUST invoke it\\\\n- Skills are located in `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`\\\\n- Never implement directly if a skill applies\\\\n- Always follow the skill instructions exactly (do not partially apply them)\\\\n\\\\n### Intent → Skill Mapping\\\\n\\\\nThe agent should automatically map user intent to skills:\\\\n\\\\n- Feature / new functionality → `spec-driven-development`, then `incremental-implementation`, `test-driven-development`\\\\n- Planning / breakdown → `planning-and-task-breakdown`\\\\n- Bug / failure / unexpected behavior → `debugging-and-error-recovery`\\\\n- Code review → `code-review-and-quality`\\\\n- Refactoring / simplification → `code-simplification`\\\\n- API or interface design → `api-and-interface-design`\\\\n- UI work → `frontend-ui-engineering`\\\\n\\\\n### Lifecycle Mapping (Implicit Commands)\\\\n\\\\nOpenCode does not support slash commands like `/spec` or `/plan`.\\\\n\\\\nInstead, the agent must internally follow this lifecycle:\\\\n\\\\n- DEFINE → `spec-driven-development`\\\\n- PLAN → `planning-and-task-breakdown`\\\\n- BUILD → `incremental-implementation` + `test-driven-development`\\\\n- VERIFY → `debugging-and-error-recovery`\\\\n- REVIEW → `code-review-and-quality`\\\\n- SHIP → `shipping-and-launch`\\\\n\\\\n### Execution Model\\\\n\\\\nFor every request:\\\\n\\\\n1. Determine if any skill applies (even 1% chance)\\\\n2. Invoke the appropriate skill using the `skill` tool\\\\n3. Follow the skill workflow strictly\\\\n4. Only proceed to implementation after required steps (spec, plan, etc.) are complete\\\\n\\\\n### Anti-Rationalization\\\\n\\\\nThe following thoughts are incorrect and must be ignored:\\\\n\\\\n- \\\\\\\"This is too small for a skill\\\\\\\"\\\\n- \\\\\\\"I can just quickly implement this\\\\\\\"\\\\n- \\\\\\\"I’ll gather context first\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nCorrect behavior:\\\\n\\\\n- Always check for and use skills first\\\\n\\\\nThis ensures OpenCode behaves similarly to Claude Code with full workflow enforcement.\\\\n\\\\n## Orchestration: Personas, Skills, and Commands\\\\n\\\\nThis repo has three composable layers. They have different jobs and should not be confused:\\\\n\\\\n- **Skills** (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — workflows with steps and exit criteria. The *how*. Mandatory hops when an intent matches.\\\\n- **Personas** (`agents/<role>.md`) — roles with a perspective and an output format. The *who*.\\\\n- **Slash commands** (`.claude/commands/*.md`) — user-facing entry points. The *when*. The orchestration layer.\\\\n\\\\nComposition rule: **the user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. Personas do not invoke other personas.** A persona may invoke skills.\\\\n\\\\nThe only multi-persona orchestration pattern this repo endorses is **parallel fan-out with a merge step** — used by `/ship` to run `code-reviewer`, `security-auditor`, and `test-engineer` concurrently and synthesize their reports. Do not build a \\\\\\\"router\\\\\\\" persona that decides which other persona to call; that's the job of slash commands and intent mapping.\\\\n\\\\nSee [agents/README.md](agents/README.md) for the decision matrix and [references/orchestration-patterns.md](references/orchestration-patterns.md) for the full pattern catalog.\\\\n\\\\n**Claude Code interop:** the personas in `agents/` work as Claude Code subagents (auto-discovered from this plugin's `agents/` directory) and as Agent Teams teammates (referenced by name when spawning). Two platform constraints align with our rules: subagents cannot spawn other subagents, and teams cannot nest. Plugin agents silently ignore the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, and `permissionMode` frontmatter fields.\\\\n\\\\n## Creating a New Skill\\\\n\\\\n### Directory Structure\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nskills/\\\\n  {skill-name}/           # kebab-case directory name\\\\n    SKILL.md              # Required: skill definition\\\\n    scripts/              # Required: executable scripts\\\\n      {script-name}.sh    # Bash scripts (preferred)\\\\n  {skill-name}.zip        # Required: packaged for distribution\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### Naming Conventions\\\\n\\\\n- **Skill directory**: `kebab-case` (e.g. `web-quality`)\\\\n- **SKILL.md**: Always uppercase, always this exact filename\\\\n- **Scripts**: `kebab-case.sh` (e.g., `deploy.sh`, `fetch-logs.sh`)\\\\n- **Zip file**: Must match directory name exactly: `{skill-name}.zip`\\\\n\\\\n### SKILL.md Format\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n---\\\\nname: {skill-name}\\\\ndescription: {One sentence describing when to use this skill. Include trigger phrases like \\\\\\\"Deploy my app\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"Check logs\\\\\\\", etc.}\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# {Skill Title}\\\\n\\\\n{Brief description of what the skill does.}\\\\n\\\\n## How It Works\\\\n\\\\n{Numbered list explaining the skill's workflow}\\\\n\\\\n## Usage\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\nbash /mnt/skills/user/{skill-name}/scripts/{script}.sh [args]\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Arguments:**\\\\n- `arg1` - Description (defaults to X)\\\\n\\\\n**Examples:**\\\\n{Show 2-3 common usage patterns}\\\\n\\\\n## Output\\\\n\\\\n{Show example output users will see}\\\\n\\\\n## Present Results to User\\\\n\\\\n{Template for how Claude should format results when presenting to users}\\\\n\\\\n## Troubleshooting\\\\n\\\\n{Common issues and solutions, especially network/permissions errors}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### Best Practices for Context Efficiency\\\\n\\\\nSkills are loaded on-demand — only the skill name and description are loaded at startup. The full `SKILL.md` loads into context only when the agent decides the skill is relevant. To minimize context usage:\\\\n\\\\n- **Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines** — put detailed reference material in separate files\\\\n- **Write specific descriptions** — helps the agent know exactly when to activate the skill\\\\n- **Use progressive disclosure** — reference supporting files that get read only when needed\\\\n- **Prefer scripts over inline code** — script execution doesn't consume context (only output does)\\\\n- **File references work one level deep** — link directly from SKILL.md to supporting files\\\\n\\\\n### Script Requirements\\\\n\\\\n- Use `#!/bin/bash` shebang\\\\n- Use `set -e` for fail-fast behavior\\\\n- Write status messages to stderr: `echo \\\\\\\"Message\\\\\\\" >&2`\\\\n- Write machine-readable output (JSON) to stdout\\\\n- Include a cleanup trap for temp files\\\\n- Reference the script path as `/mnt/skills/user/{skill-name}/scripts/{script}.sh`\\\\n\\\\n### Creating the Zip Package\\\\n\\\\nAfter creating or updating a skill:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\ncd skills\\\\nzip -r {skill-name}.zip {skill-name}/\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### End-User Installation\\\\n\\\\nDocument these two installation methods for users:\\\\n\\\\n**Claude Code:**\\\\n```bash\\\\ncp -r skills/{skill-name} ~/.claude/skills/\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**claude.ai:**\\\\nAdd the skill to project knowledge or paste SKILL.md contents into the conversation.\\\\n\\\\nIf the skill requires network access, instruct users to add required domains at `claude.ai/settings/capabilities`.\\\\n\\\",\\n  \\\"encoding\\\": \\\"base64\\\",\\n  \\\"_links\\\": {\\n    \\\"self\\\": \\\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/main/references/orchestration-patterns.md\\\",\\n  \\\"type\\\": \\\"file\\\",\\n  \\\"content\\\": \\\"# Orchestration Patterns\\\\n\\\\nReference catalog of agent orchestration patterns this repo endorses, plus anti-patterns to avoid. Read this before adding a new slash command that coordinates multiple personas, or before introducing a new persona that \\\\\\\"wraps\\\\\\\" existing ones.\\\\n\\\\nThe governing rule: **the user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. Personas do not invoke other personas.** Skills are mandatory hops inside a persona's workflow.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Endorsed patterns\\\\n\\\\n### 1. Direct invocation (no orchestration)\\\\n\\\\nSingle persona, single perspective, single artifact. The default and the cheapest option.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nuser → code-reviewer → report → user\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the work is one perspective on one artifact and you can describe it in one sentence.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples:**\\\\n- \\\\\\\"Review this PR\\\\\\\" → `code-reviewer`\\\\n- \\\\\\\"Find security issues in `auth.ts`\\\\\\\" → `security-auditor`\\\\n- \\\\\\\"What tests are missing for the checkout flow?\\\\\\\" → `test-engineer`\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one round trip. The baseline you should always compare orchestrated patterns against.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 2. Single-persona slash command\\\\n\\\\nA slash command that wraps one persona with the project's skills. Saves the user from re-explaining the workflow every time.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n/review → code-reviewer (with code-review-and-quality skill) → report\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the same single-persona invocation happens repeatedly with the same setup.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/review`, `/test`, `/code-simplify`.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** same as direct invocation. The slash command is just a saved prompt.\\\\n\\\\n**Anti-signal:** if the slash command's body is mostly \\\\\\\"decide which persona to call,\\\\\\\" delete it and let the user call the persona directly.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 3. Parallel fan-out with merge\\\\n\\\\nMultiple personas operate on the same input concurrently, each producing an independent report. A merge step (in the main agent's context) synthesizes them into a single decision.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n                    ┌─→ code-reviewer    ─┐\\\\n/ship → fan out  ───┼─→ security-auditor ─┤→ merge → go/no-go + rollback\\\\n                    └─→ test-engineer    ─┘\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\n- The sub-tasks are genuinely independent (no shared mutable state, no ordering dependency)\\\\n- Each sub-agent benefits from its own context window\\\\n- The merge step is small enough to stay in the main context\\\\n- Wall-clock latency matters\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** `/ship`.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** N parallel sub-agent contexts + one merge turn. Higher than direct invocation, but faster wall-clock and produces better reports because each sub-agent stays focused on its single perspective.\\\\n\\\\n**Validation checklist before adopting this pattern:**\\\\n- [ ] Can I run all sub-agents at the same time without ordering issues?\\\\n- [ ] Does each persona produce a different *kind* of finding, not just the same finding from a different angle?\\\\n- [ ] Will the merge step fit in the main agent's remaining context?\\\\n- [ ] Is the user's wait time long enough that parallelism is actually noticeable?\\\\n\\\\nIf any answer is \\\\\\\"no,\\\\\\\" fall back to direct invocation or a single-persona command.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 4. Sequential pipeline as user-driven slash commands\\\\n\\\\nThe user runs slash commands in a defined order, carrying context (or commit history) between them. There is no orchestrator agent — the user IS the orchestrator.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nuser runs:  /spec  →  /plan  →  /build  →  /test  →  /review  →  /ship\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:** the workflow has dependencies (each step needs the previous step's output) and human judgment between steps adds value.\\\\n\\\\n**Examples in this repo:** the entire DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP lifecycle.\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one sub-agent context per step. Free for the orchestration layer because there is no orchestrator agent.\\\\n\\\\n**Why not automate it:** an LLM \\\\\\\"lifecycle orchestrator\\\\\\\" would (a) lose nuance between steps because it has to summarize for hand-off, (b) skip the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work early, and (c) double the token cost via paraphrasing turns.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 5. Research isolation (context preservation)\\\\n\\\\nWhen a task requires reading large amounts of material that shouldn't pollute the main context, spawn a research sub-agent that returns only a digest.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nmain agent → research sub-agent (reads 50 files) → digest → main agent continues\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Use when:**\\\\n- The main session needs to stay focused on a downstream task\\\\n- The investigation result is much smaller than the input it consumes\\\\n- The decision quality benefits from the main agent having room to think after\\\\n\\\\n**Examples:** \\\\\\\"Find every call site of this deprecated API across the monorepo,\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\"Summarize what these 30 ADRs say about caching.\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n**Cost:** one isolated sub-agent context. Worth it any time the alternative is loading hundreds of files into the main context.\\\\n\\\\n**On Claude Code, use the built-in `Explore` subagent** rather than defining a custom research persona. `Explore` runs on Haiku, is denied write/edit tools, and is purpose-built for this pattern. Define a custom research subagent only when `Explore` doesn't fit (e.g. you need a domain-specific system prompt the model wouldn't infer).\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Claude Code compatibility\\\\n\\\\nThis catalog is harness-agnostic, but most readers will run it on Claude Code. Here's how each pattern maps onto Claude Code's primitives — and where the platform enforces our rules for us.\\\\n\\\\n### Where personas live\\\\n\\\\nPlugin subagents go in `agents/` at the plugin root. This repo is a plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), so `agents/code-reviewer.md`, `agents/security-auditor.md`, and `agents/test-engineer.md` are auto-discovered when the plugin is enabled. No path configuration needed.\\\\n\\\\n### Subagents vs. Agent Teams\\\\n\\\\nClaude Code has two parallelism primitives. Pattern 3 (parallel fan-out with merge) maps to **subagents**. If you need teammates that talk to each other, use **Agent Teams** instead.\\\\n\\\\n| | Subagents | Agent Teams |\\\\n|--|-----------|-------------|\\\\n| Coordination | Main agent fans out, sub-agents only report back | Teammates message each other, share a task list |\\\\n| Context | Own context window per subagent | Own context window per teammate |\\\\n| When to use | Independent tasks producing reports | Collaborative work needing discussion |\\\\n| Status | Stable | Experimental — requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` |\\\\n| Cost | Lower | Higher — each teammate is a separate Claude instance |\\\\n\\\\n**The personas in this repo work in both modes.** When spawned as subagents (e.g. by `/ship`), they report findings to the main session. When spawned as teammates (`Spawn a teammate using the security-auditor agent type…`), they can challenge each other's findings directly. The persona definition is the same; only the spawning context changes.\\\\n\\\\nOne subtlety: the `skills` and `mcpServers` frontmatter fields in a persona are honored when it runs as a subagent but **ignored when it runs as a teammate** — teammates load skills and MCP servers from your project and user settings, the same as a regular session. If a persona depends on a specific skill or MCP server being loaded, configure it at the session level so it's available in both modes.\\\\n\\\\n### Platform-enforced rules\\\\n\\\\nTwo rules in this catalog aren't just convention — Claude Code enforces them:\\\\n\\\\n- **\\\\\\\"Subagents cannot spawn other subagents\\\\\\\"** (verbatim from the docs). Anti-pattern B (persona-calls-persona) and Anti-pattern D (deep persona trees) cannot exist on Claude Code by construction.\\\\n- **\\\\\\\"No nested teams\\\\\\\"** — teammates cannot spawn their own teams. Same anti-patterns blocked at the team level.\\\\n\\\\nThis means you can adopt the patterns in this catalog without worrying about contributors accidentally building the anti-patterns. They'll just fail to load.\\\\n\\\\n### Built-in subagents to know about\\\\n\\\\nBefore defining a custom subagent, check whether one of these covers the role:\\\\n\\\\n| Built-in | Purpose |\\\\n|----------|---------|\\\\n| `Explore` | Read-only codebase search and analysis. Use this for Pattern 5 (research isolation). |\\\\n| `Plan` | Read-only research during plan mode. |\\\\n| `general-purpose` | Multi-step tasks needing both exploration and modification. |\\\\n\\\\nDon't redefine these. Layer your specialist personas (code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-engineer) on top of them.\\\\n\\\\n### Frontmatter restrictions for plugin agents\\\\n\\\\nPlugin subagents do **not** support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields — these are silently ignored. If a future persona needs any of those, the user must copy the file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` instead.\\\\n\\\\nThe fields that DO work in plugin agents are: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `memory`, `background`, `effort`, `isolation`, `color`, `initialPrompt`. Use `model` per-persona if you want to optimize cost (e.g. Haiku for `test-engineer` coverage scans, Sonnet for `code-reviewer`, Opus for `security-auditor`).\\\\n\\\\n### Spawning multiple subagents in parallel\\\\n\\\\nIn Claude Code, parallel fan-out (Pattern 3) requires issuing **multiple Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn**. Sequential turns serialize execution. `/ship` calls this out explicitly. Any new orchestrator command should do the same.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Worked example: Agent Teams for competing-hypothesis debugging\\\\n\\\\nThis example shows when to reach for **Agent Teams** instead of `/ship`'s subagent fan-out. The two patterns look similar from a distance — both spawn the same three personas — but the value comes from a different place.\\\\n\\\\n### The scenario\\\\n\\\\n> *Checkout occasionally hangs for ~30 seconds before completing. It happens roughly once every 50 sessions. No errors in logs. Started after last week's release.*\\\\n\\\\nPlausible root causes (mutually exclusive, all fit the symptoms):\\\\n\\\\n1. A race condition in the new payment-confirmation flow\\\\n2. An auth check that occasionally falls through to a slow synchronous network call\\\\n3. A missing index on a query that scales with cart size\\\\n4. A flaky third-party API where the SDK retries silently before timing out\\\\n\\\\nA single agent will pick the first plausible theory and stop investigating. A `/ship`-style subagent fan-out would have each persona report independently — but their reports never meet, so nothing rules out the wrong theories.\\\\n\\\\nThis is exactly the case the Agent Teams docs describe: *\\\\\\\"With multiple independent investigators actively trying to disprove each other, the theory that survives is much more likely to be the actual root cause.\\\\\\\"*\\\\n\\\\n### Why this is *not* a `/ship` job\\\\n\\\\n| | `/ship` (subagents) | Agent Teams |\\\\n|--|--------------------|-------------|\\\\n| Sub-agents see | The same diff, different lenses | A shared task list, each other's messages |\\\\n| Output | Three independent reports → one merge | Adversarial debate → consensus root cause |\\\\n| Right when | You want a verdict on a known artifact | You want to *find* the artifact among hypotheses |\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` is a verdict; Agent Teams is an investigation.\\\\n\\\\n### Setup (one-time, per-environment)\\\\n\\\\nAgent Teams is experimental. In `~/.claude/settings.json`:\\\\n\\\\n```json\\\\n{\\\\n  \\\\\\\"env\\\\\\\": {\\\\n    \\\\\\\"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"1\\\\\\\"\\\\n  }\\\\n}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nRequires Claude Code v2.1.32 or later. The personas in this repo are picked up automatically — no team-config files to author by hand.\\\\n\\\\n### The trigger prompt\\\\n\\\\nType into the lead session, in natural language:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nUsers report checkout hangs for ~30 seconds intermittently after last\\\\nweek's release. No errors in logs.\\\\n\\\\nCreate an agent team to debug this with competing hypotheses. Spawn\\\\nthree teammates using the existing agent types:\\\\n\\\\n  - code-reviewer  — investigate race conditions and blocking calls\\\\n                     in the checkout code path\\\\n  - security-auditor — investigate auth checks, session handling,\\\\n                       and any synchronous network calls added recently\\\\n  - test-engineer  — propose tests that would distinguish between the\\\\n                     hypotheses and check coverage gaps in checkout\\\\n\\\\nHave them message each other directly to challenge each other's\\\\ntheories. Update findings as consensus emerges. Only converge when\\\\ntwo teammates agree they can disprove the others'.\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe lead spawns three teammates referencing the existing persona names. The persona body is **appended** to each teammate's system prompt as additional instructions (on top of the team-coordination instructions the lead installs); the trigger prompt above becomes their task.\\\\n\\\\n### What happens\\\\n\\\\n1. Each teammate runs in its own context window, exploring the codebase from its own lens.\\\\n2. Teammates use `message` to send findings to each other directly. The lead doesn't have to relay.\\\\n3. The shared task list shows who's investigating what — visible at any time with `Ctrl+T` (in-process mode) or in a tmux pane (split mode).\\\\n4. When `code-reviewer` finds a `Promise.all` that should be sequential, it messages `security-auditor` to confirm the auth call isn't part of the race. `security-auditor` checks and replies — either confirming the race is the real issue or producing counter-evidence.\\\\n5. `test-engineer` proposes a focused integration test for whichever theory is winning, which the team uses to verify before declaring consensus.\\\\n6. The lead synthesizes the converged finding and presents it to you.\\\\n\\\\nYou can interrupt at any teammate by cycling with `Shift+Down` and typing — useful for redirecting an investigator who's gone down a wrong path.\\\\n\\\\n### When to clean up\\\\n\\\\nWhen the investigation lands on a root cause, tell the lead:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nClean up the team\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAlways cleanup through the lead, not a teammate (per the docs: teammates lack full team context for cleanup).\\\\n\\\\n### Cost expectation\\\\n\\\\nThree Sonnet teammates running for ~10–15 minutes of investigation costs noticeably more than the same three personas spawned as subagents by `/ship`. The justification is *quality of conclusion* — for production debugging where the wrong fix is expensive, the extra tokens are a bargain. For a routine PR review, stick with `/ship`.\\\\n\\\\n### Anti-pattern in this scenario\\\\n\\\\nDo **not** rebuild this as a `/debug` slash command that fans out subagents. Subagents can't message each other — you'd lose the adversarial debate that makes the pattern work. If a workflow keeps coming up, document the trigger prompt above as a snippet rather than wrapping it in a slash command that misuses subagents.\\\\n\\\\n### When *not* to use Agent Teams\\\\n\\\\n- Production-bound verdict on a known diff → use `/ship` (subagents).\\\\n- One specialist perspective on one artifact → direct persona invocation.\\\\n- Sequential lifecycle (spec → plan → build) → user-driven slash commands (Pattern 4).\\\\n- Read-heavy research with a small digest → built-in `Explore` subagent.\\\\n\\\\nReach for Agent Teams only when teammates **need** to challenge each other to produce the right answer.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Anti-patterns\\\\n\\\\n### A. Router persona (\\\\\\\"meta-orchestrator\\\\\\\")\\\\n\\\\nA persona whose job is to decide which other persona to call.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n/work → router-persona → \\\\\\\"this needs a review\\\\\\\" → code-reviewer → router (paraphrases) → user\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Pure routing layer with no domain value\\\\n- Adds two paraphrasing hops → information loss + roughly 2× token cost\\\\n- The user already knew they wanted a review; they could have called `/review` directly\\\\n- Replicates the work that slash commands and intent mapping in `AGENTS.md` already do\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** add or refine slash commands. Document intent → command mapping in `AGENTS.md`.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### B. Persona that calls another persona\\\\n\\\\nA `code-reviewer` that internally invokes `security-auditor` when it sees auth code.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Personas were designed to produce a single perspective; chaining them defeats that\\\\n- The summary the calling persona passes loses context the called persona needs\\\\n- Failure modes multiply (which persona's output format wins? whose rules apply?)\\\\n- Hides cost from the user\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** have the calling persona *recommend* a follow-up audit in its report. The user or a slash command runs the second pass.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### C. Sequential orchestrator that paraphrases\\\\n\\\\nAn agent that calls `/spec`, then `/plan`, then `/build`, etc. on the user's behalf.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Loses the human checkpoints that catch wrong-direction work\\\\n- Each hand-off summarizes context — accumulated drift over a long pipeline\\\\n- Doubles token cost: orchestrator turn + sub-agent turn for every step\\\\n- Removes user agency at exactly the points where judgment matters most\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the user as the orchestrator. Document the recommended sequence in `README.md` and let users invoke it.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### D. Deep persona trees\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` calls a `pre-ship-coordinator` that calls a `quality-coordinator` that calls `code-reviewer`.\\\\n\\\\n**Why it fails:**\\\\n- Each layer adds latency and tokens with no decision value\\\\n- Debugging becomes a multi-level investigation\\\\n- The leaf personas lose context to multiple summarization steps\\\\n\\\\n**What to do instead:** keep the orchestration depth at most 1 (slash command → personas). The merge happens in the main agent.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Decision flow\\\\n\\\\nWhen considering a new orchestrated workflow, walk this flow:\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nIs the work one perspective on one artifact?\\\\n├── Yes → Direct invocation. Stop.\\\\n└── No  → Will the same composition repeat?\\\\n         ├── No  → Direct invocation, ad hoc. Stop.\\\\n         └── Yes → Are sub-tasks independent?\\\\n                  ├── No  → Sequential slash commands run by user (Pattern 4).\\\\n                  └── Yes → Parallel fan-out with merge (Pattern 3).\\\\n                           Validate against the checklist above.\\\\n                           If any check fails → fall back to single-persona command (Pattern 2).\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## When to add a new pattern to this catalog\\\\n\\\\nAdd a new entry only after:\\\\n\\\\n1. You've used the pattern at least twice in real work\\\\n2. You can name a concrete artifact in this repo that demonstrates it\\\\n3. You can explain why an existing pattern wouldn't have worked\\\\n4. You can describe its anti-pattern shadow (what people will mistakenly build instead)\\\\n\\\\nPremature catalog entries become aspirational documentation that no one follows.\\\\n\\\",\\n \\\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/main/.claude/commands/ship.md\\\",\\n  \\\"type\\\": \\\"file\\\",\\n  \\\"content\\\": \\\"---\\\\ndescription: Run the pre-launch checklist via parallel fan-out to specialist personas, then synthesize a go/no-go decision\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\nInvoke the agent-skills:shipping-and-launch skill.\\\\n\\\\n`/ship` is a **fan-out orchestrator**. It runs three specialist personas in parallel against the current change, then merges their reports into a single go/no-go decision with a rollback plan. The personas operate independently — no shared state, no ordering — which is what makes parallel execution safe and useful here.\\\\n\\\\n## Phase A — Parallel fan-out\\\\n\\\\nSpawn three subagents concurrently using the Agent tool. **Issue all three Agent tool calls in a single assistant turn so they execute in parallel** — sequential calls defeat the purpose of this command.\\\\n\\\\nIn Claude Code, each call passes `subagent_type` matching the persona's `name` field:\\\\n\\\\n1. **`code-reviewer`** — Run a five-axis review (correctness, readability, architecture, security, performance) on the staged changes or recent commits. Output the standard review template.\\\\n2. **`security-auditor`** — Run a vulnerability and threat-model pass. Check OWASP Top 10, secrets handling, auth/authz, dependency CVEs. Output the standard audit report.\\\\n3. **`test-engineer`** — Analyze test coverage for the change. Identify gaps in happy path, edge cases, error paths, and concurrency scenarios. Output the standard coverage analysis.\\\\n\\\\nIn other harnesses without an Agent tool, invoke each persona's system prompt sequentially and treat their outputs as if returned in parallel — the merge phase still works.\\\\n\\\\nConstraints (from Claude Code's subagent model):\\\\n- Subagents cannot spawn other subagents — do not let one persona delegate to another.\\\\n- Each subagent gets its own context window and returns only its report to this main session.\\\\n- If you need teammates that talk to each other instead of just reporting back, use Claude Code Agent Teams and reference these personas as teammate types (see `references/orchestration-patterns.md`).\\\\n\\\\n**Persona resolution.** If you've defined your own `code-reviewer`, `security-auditor`, or `test-engineer` in `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/`, those take precedence over this plugin's versions — `/ship` picks up your customizations automatically. This is intentional: plugin subagents sit at the bottom of Claude Code's scope priority table, so user-level definitions win by design.\\\\n\\\\n## Phase B — Merge in main context\\\\n\\\\nOnce all three reports are back, the main agent (not a sub-persona) synthesizes them:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Code Quality** — Aggregate Critical/Important findings from `code-reviewer` and any failing tests, lint, or build output. Resolve duplicates between reviewers.\\\\n2. **Security** — Promote any Critical/High `security-auditor` findings to launch blockers. Cross-reference with `code-reviewer`'s security axis.\\\\n3. **Performance** — Pull from `code-reviewer`'s performance axis; cross-check Core Web Vitals if applicable.\\\\n4. **Accessibility** — Verify keyboard nav, screen reader support, contrast (not covered by the three personas — handle directly here, or invoke the accessibility checklist).\\\\n5. **Infrastructure** — Env vars, migrations, monitoring, feature flags. Verify directly.\\\\n6. **Documentation** — README, ADRs, changelog. Verify directly.\\\\n\\\\n## Phase C — Decision and rollback\\\\n\\\\nProduce a single output:\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n## Ship Decision: GO | NO-GO\\\\n\\\\n### Blockers (must fix before ship)\\\\n- [Source persona: Critical finding + file:line]\\\\n\\\\n### Recommended fixes (should fix before ship)\\\\n- [Source persona: Important finding + file:line]\\\\n\\\\n### Acknowledged risks (shipping anyway)\\\\n- [Risk + mitigation]\\\\n\\\\n### Rollback plan\\\\n- Trigger conditions: [what signals would prompt rollback]\\\\n- Rollback procedure: [exact steps]\\\\n- Recovery time objective: [target]\\\\n\\\\n### Specialist reports (full)\\\\n- [code-reviewer report]\\\\n- [security-auditor report]\\\\n- [test-engineer report]\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Rules\\\\n\\\\n1. The three Phase A personas run in parallel — never sequentially.\\\\n2. Personas do not call each other. The main agent merges in Phase B.\\\\n3. The rollback plan is mandatory before any GO decision.\\\\n4. If any persona returns a Critical finding, the default verdict is NO-GO unless the user explicitly accepts the risk.\\\\n5. **Skip the fan-out only if all of the following are true:** the change touches 2 files or fewer, the diff is under 50 lines, and it does not touch auth, payments, data access, or config/env. Otherwise, default to fan-out. `/ship` is designed for production-bound changes — when the blast radius is non-trivial, run the parallel review even if the diff looks small.\\\\n\\\",\\n Skills are packaged instructions and scripts that extend Claude and your coding agents capabilities.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## OpenCode Integration\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nOpenCode uses a **skill-driven execution model** powered by the `skill` tool and this repository's `/skills` directory.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Core Rules\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- If a task matches a skill, you MUST invoke it\\\\\\\\n- Skills are located in `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`\\\\\\\\n- Never implement directly if a skill applies\\\\\\\\n- Always follow the skill instructions exactly (do not partially apply them)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Intent → Skill Mapping\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe agent should automatically map user intent to skills:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- Feature / new functionality → `spec-driven-development`, then `incremental-implementation`, `test-driven-development`\\\\\\\\n- Planning / breakdown → `planning-and-task-breakdown`\\\\\\\\n- Bug / failure / unexpected behavior → `debugging-and-error-recovery`\\\\\\\\n- Code review → `code-review-and-quality`\\\\\\\\n- Refactoring / simplification → `code-simplification`\\\\\\\\n- API or interface design → `api-and-interface-design`\\\\\\\\n- UI work → `frontend-ui-engineering`\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Lifecycle Mapping (Implicit Commands)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nOpenCode does not support slash commands like `/spec` or `/plan`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nInstead, the agent must internally follow this lifecycle:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- DEFINE → `spec-driven-development`\\\\\\\\n- PLAN → `planning-and-task-breakdown`\\\\\\\\n- BUILD → `incremental-implementation` + `test-driven-development`\\\\\\\\n- VERIFY → `debugging-and-error-recovery`\\\\\\\\n- REVIEW → `code-review-and-quality`\\\\\\\\n- SHIP → `shipping-and-launch`\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Execution Model\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nFor every request:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. Determine if any skill applies (even 1% chance)\\\\\\\\n2. Invoke the appropriate skill using the `skill` tool\\\\\\\\n3. Follow the skill workflow strictly\\\\\\\\n4. Only proceed to implementation after required steps (spec, plan, etc.) are complete\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Anti-Rationalization\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe following thoughts are incorrect and must be ignored:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"This is too small for a skill\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n- \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"I can just quickly implement this\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n- \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"I’ll gather context first\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nCorrect behavior:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- Always check for and use skills first\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis ensures OpenCode behaves similarly to Claude Code with full workflow enforcement.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Orchestration: Personas, Skills, and Commands\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThis repo has three composable layers. They have different jobs and should not be confused:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- **Skills** (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — workflows with steps and exit criteria. The *how*. Mandatory hops when an intent matches.\\\\\\\\n- **Personas** (`agents/<role>.md`) — roles with a perspective and an output format. The *who*.\\\\\\\\n- **Slash commands** (`.claude/commands/*.md`) — user-facing entry points. The *when*. The orchestration layer.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nComposition rule: **the user (or a slash command) is the orchestrator. Personas do not invoke other personas.** A persona may invoke skills.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe only multi-persona orchestration pattern this repo endorses is **parallel fan-out with a merge step** — used by `/ship` to run `code-reviewer`, `security-auditor`, and `test-engineer` concurrently and synthesize their reports. Do not build a \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"router\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" persona that decides which other persona to call; that's the job of slash commands and intent mapping.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nSee [agents/README.md](agents/README.md) for the decision matrix and [references/orchestration-patterns.md](references/orchestration-patterns.md) for the full pattern catalog.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Claude Code interop:** the personas in `agents/` work as Claude Code subagents (auto-discovered from this plugin's `agents/` directory) and as Agent Teams teammates (referenced by name when spawning). Two platform constraints align with our rules: subagents cannot spawn other subagents, and teams cannot nest. Plugin agents silently ignore the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, and `permissionMode` frontmatter fields.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Creating a New Skill\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Directory Structure\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\nskills/\\\\\\\\n  {skill-name}/           # kebab-case directory name\\\\\\\\n    SKILL.md              # Required: skill definition\\\\\\\\n    scripts/              # Required: executable scripts\\\\\\\\n      {script-name}.sh    # Bash scripts (preferred)\\\\\\\\n  {skill-name}.zip        # Required: packaged for distribution\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Naming Conventions\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- **Skill directory**: `kebab-case` (e.g. `web-quality`)\\\\\\\\n- **SKILL.md**: Always uppercase, always this exact filename\\\\\\\\n- **Scripts**: `kebab-case.sh` (e.g., `deploy.sh`, `fetch-logs.sh`)\\\\\\\\n- **Zip file**: Must match directory name exactly: `{skill-name}.zip`\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### SKILL.md Format\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```markdown\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\nname: {skill-name}\\\\\\\\ndescription: {One sentence describing when to use this skill.
